subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-PICTURE AND ARTICLE IN MONTREAL "GAZETTE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise on a question of privilege so there will be no misconception or distortion by misrepresentation later on as to what took place. I warn hon. members against accepting at face value a report appearing along with a photograph in this morning's Montreal Gazette to the effect that I explained certain matters of public interest to a meeting in the city of Ottawa from a rostrum described as being "draped with a union jack".
I have no objection to the picture, in which I am as attractive as I am usually depicted to be. But I would point out that the flag on the rostrum was the red ensign, though the only portion shown in the picture is that portion of the red ensign which consists of the union jack. With the statement that I had discussed certain issues of public affairs before a fine audience which gave close attention, I am in agreement, but the flag in question was the red ensign authorized by order in council in April, 1945, and continued since as the Canadian flag in general use within Canada and throughout the world.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

Hon. Guy Favreau (Minister of Justice).
Mr. Speaker, before prescription comes into effect and I lose my right to do so, I should like to answer the question put on May 12 last by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) concerning the remission of lash sentences at the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary and the right of the parole board to remit or change those penalties.
Under section 18, paragraph (1) of the Parole Act, the parole board has the right to revoke or suspend sentences to the lash passed under the Criminal Code.
When a request for the suspension or repeal of a sentence to the lash is submitted to the board and the board orders an inquiry, the sentence is usually suspended while the inquiry is in progress. At the conclusion of the inquiry, the board's decision is made known to the warden of the jail where the prisoner who has applied for a remission is held, and the warden must then carry out the penalty of the lash if the board refused to remit the sentence.

Inquiries of the Ministry
During the first 64 months of operation, the board received 24 requests to remit the penalty of the lash. Of these, eight were granted and 16 refused.
The board has received eight requests during the year 1964, four of which came from the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, and they were refused.

Mr. Chairman, while I was away from the house the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Agriculture on May 15 again spoke to a matter which I raised initially in the debate on April 24. I will not take much of the time of the committee today, but I think some of the remarks made by both the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Agriculture deserve some comment.
You will recall that at that time an affidavit of Mr. McKay was tabled as sessional paper No. 249, a copy of which I have before me, and the affidavit of Mr. McKay would appear to be at variance with the situation as I described it partly on April 24 and partly on May 7. The Minister of Agriculture said on May 15, as found on page 3311 of Hansard:
I told the house several times that the hon. member's claims-
Referring to myself.
-were entirely without foundation.
He had something to say about the tactics which I employed in introducing this matter

in the committee, and made certain other references about which I will not go into detail at this time. But the interesting portion of the minister's remarks is found on page 3312 of Hansard for that date in the left hand column, where he is reported as having said:
Our investigations also confirmed that neither I nor my officials requested that the contract be interfered with.
That is the contract with Purity Dairy.
I have, however, since May 7 learned of a matter which I did not know on that date but for which I, as the minister, take full responsibility.
This is the important sentence.
This in no way changes any earlier statement...
The matter to which the minister refers as having learned about subsequent to May 7 is the matter of requests made of Mr. Trach to cut the contract from six months to three months. As found on page 3020 of Hansard of May 7, which was well prior to the minister's statement I have just read from Hansard of May 15, he had this to say commencing at the foot of the left hand column:
I now wish to inform him that neither I nor my officials were in any way involved in contracts with the Purity Dairy for the supply of dairy products to the R.C.A.F. station Namao or the army station at Griesbach, and that at no time did I or my officials have discussions with Jacob Trach or any other member of the Purity Dairy firm with respect to those contracts.
Also on May 7 the Minister of Industry, as found on page 3021 of Hansard, said substantially the same thing; that there had been no discussions with Mr. Trach and no attempt at interference with the running of the full term of the contract. The Minister of Industry challenged me on May 15 to produce an affidavit from Mr. Trach. He also did so, of course, on May 7. He questioned my rising in the committee and making statements which he said were utterly without foundation, and on May 15 the Minister of Agriculture referred to the statements as completely false, utterly false and used other similar descriptions. I think "patently false" was another phrase the minister used.
The Minister of Industry went on to say, as found on page 3314 of Hansard of May 15:
...and I challenge the hon. member for Yukon to produce an affidavit from Mr. Trach to the contrary effect. I regret that he has been unable to do this, and perhaps in the light of his inability to do so he will withdraw his remarks.
Sir, I have for the benefit of the committee just such an affidavit, and I am going to read it. While it is perhaps not possible for members to compare the affidavits at this

time, certainly when they have the record before them they will be able to compare Mr. Trach's affidavit made under oath with that of Mr. McKay to see whether in fact I had any justification for raising the matter as I did, not as a charge but as a matter in which I felt the committee should interest itself since it involved the activities of both the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Agriculture. Mr. Trach's affidavit reads as follows:
In a matter of a certain dairy contract between Purity Dairy and defence production and in particular with Greisbach barracks and station Namao.
Affidavit of Trach
I,	Jacob Trach, of the city of Edmonton, manager, make oath and say as follows:
1.	That I am the manager of the Purity Dairy Company in the city of Edmonton and therefore have personal knowledge of the facts deposed by me, except where stated on information and belief.
2.	That Purity Dairy Company, my firm, had and have a contract in reference to milk and ice cream with defence production to supply for a period of six months milk and ice cream to Greisbach barracks and station Namao and which contract was for the months of October, 1963 to March of 1964 inclusive.
3. Late in October of 1963 a McKay of defence production telephoned me at the Purity plant in Edmonton and we had a telephone conversation in reference to the said six month milk and ice cream contract in question.
4. In brief the said McKay said that he had been approached by Ottawa authorities in the department, and at that moment he didn't mention names, requesting that the said Purity contract with defence production be cut to three months. He stated there were certain pressures being applied and because of the said pressure he wanted the Purity Dairy Company to agree to have the contract changed from a six month one to a three month one.
5.	In the same said telephone conversation I, as manager of Purity Dairy Company wanted to know under what circumstances and what legal right defence production had the right to cut our contract from six months to three. I told him this was very disturbing and that I would like to talk to him personally.
6.	In the said conversation an appointment was arranged at the said Mr. McKay's office for some time in November of 1963.
7.	I went early in November 1963 to the said Mr. McKay's office in the federal building, Edmonton, and a discussion between the said McKay and myself took place. There was no one present during this discussion.
In this regard I would refer the minister and members of the committee to paragraph 7 of Mr. McKay's affidavit.
8.	The context of the conversation which took place during the said appointment in November 1963 in the federal building in McKay's office is as follows :
He told me that there were certain elements and certain people who stated that if we did not go for a three month contract (that is to reduce the said six month contract to three) the Depart-
Supply-Agriculture
ment of Agriculture could make it very tough for us. He then referred to the federal Department of Agriculture at Ottawa, and in particular minister Hays. He stated he had instructions that the minister wanted the contract cut. I told him that in our opinion the said department in question could not break the contract as it was in writing and properly executed. He said there was a group of lawyers in Ottawa looking into the validity of the contract. It was just after that he mentioned the said lawyers in question that he said minister Hays, the Minister of Agriculture and the Department of Agriculture were going to take the contract from us, or at least reduce it from six to three months. Then he said, "We could, in accordance with instructions from Ottawa, find something wrong with your product, the milk in question. And from this pressure the department would make Purity Dairy Company agree to a new contract or to cancel the one it has." This would force our will.
9.	The said Mr. McKay said, "I do not like to bring this up in reference to having your product declared unfit, but it is my superiors and the Minister of Agriculture in Ottawa that I take my instructions from."
10.	I took it from those said statements of the said McKay that he meant his instructions came from minister Hays, the Minister of Agriculture, and the Department of Agriculture.
11.	Our company did not bow to this pressure and have continued to supply milk and ice cream to both Greisbach and Namao and have since been advised by the said McKay that contracts will be rotated between various dairies when our contract has expired, all of which I verily believe to be true.
12.	I only had one interview with the said Mr. McKay in his office at the federal building where the said abovementioned conversation took place and that interview lasted approximately 45 minutes and it took place in the early part of November. 1963.
Sworn before me at the city of Edmonton, province of Alberta-
Here, Mr. Chairman, I would ask committee members to note the date, to determine whether I had justification for raising this matter at the time I did:
-this 26th day of March, 1964.
This affidavit was sworn before a commissioner for oaths in and for the province of Alberta and it bears the notary's official seal as a notary public in and for the province of Alberta. The affidavit is signed "Jacob Trach".
With the unanimous consent of the committee, should they so desire I am fully prepared to table the document in question.
Agreed.

These charges, as I stated when I first raised the matter on April 24, were serious indeed. I put it to the committee at that time that the circumstances which I described were based on information that I had, and I took it upon my responsibility as a member of the committee to say that I had made certain that they
,3738

Supply-Agriculture
were not frivolous charges at all. I invited the minister to' give an explanation after investigating this matter, and I said at the time-1 think he will recall this-that I would hope his investigations would exonerate him and his officials. He has made a statement or an explanation on information supplied to him and the Minister of Industry by Mr. McKay, information which committee members will have no alternative but to conclude is at direct variance with the sworn affidavit of Mr. Trach.
For instance, Mr. McKay says that at no time did any discussion take place in his office between himself and Mr. Trach. There is one conflict. I invite the minister to peruse very carefully Mr. McKay's affidavit, and I think he will find it is quite conflicting both within itself and with the affidavit of Mr. Trach. Those circumstances, I feel, should be investigated by the departments concerned, and I think this committee will perhaps come to the same conclusion now.
The minister's explanation on May 15 concluded with his assertion that he wanted to see patronage eliminated in his department and in government. If that is so, why should Mr. McKay say he had received instructions, as he did in his affidavit, from the department in Ottawa to rotate the contracts? This still involves the method of selection. He said it was his practice to award contracts on the basis of the lowest cost. The only way you can get the lowest cost is to invite public tenders; and the practice in the department now is to rotate those contracts, not by inviting public tender calls but by selecting the dairy or concern that is going to supply the milk to these various users. Surely the only way to get rid of patronage in the minister's department is by inviting public tenders when requirements exist for the supply of goods and services to the government. If the minister is really serious and sincere about wanting to get rid of patronage in his department that is precisely what he will do, and eliminate or end this practice of rotating contracts to individuals or individual firms and corporations.
In the light of the affidavit which I have just read into the record and which, as I say, I will table if that is the desire of the committee, I submit to the committee through you, Mr. Chairman, that the information I supplied to the house on April 24 and on May 7 was information that I was fully justified in providing to this committee; and it was not in keeping with the proper usages

of the committee or of the house for the Minister of Industry or the Minister of Agriculture to question my motive in presenting that information to the house.
I took it upon myself, as a responsible member, to put these matters before the ministers, and I did so. Because these two ministers thought I could not substantiate in any way the information I placed before the committee they became all-incensed and made charges about my tactics and my motivations in placing this information before the committee. But I invite the minister again to look at the date of that affidavit sworn by Mr. Trach-March 26-well before I raised the matter on April 24. I invite him too, sir, to reconsider the error of his ways, and when members in all sincerity and seriousness bring irregularities such as these before the committee he should take cognizance of them and not immediately jump to the conclusion, as he did, that there was nothing wrong in the situation I presented to him.
In fact both he and the Minister of Industry, subsequent to April 24 and well before May 15, made complete denials before they had information which would have placed them in possession of all the facts. The minister expressed some surprise to learn that an approach had even been made to Mr. Trach to cut the contract from six months to three months, but he has found out since that this was the fact. I invite him now to scrutinize very carefully what Mr. Trach has had to say under oath, and said under oath well before the matter was raised in this committee.

Mr. Chairman, we have two affidavits, one by Mr. McKay denying all these things and another by Mr. Trach saying they are correct. My position is that I think the house and all hon. members know what I have said, and I still feel exactly the same way. I am the Minister of Agriculture. I suppose, being a minister, you must expect some of these things. They tell me these things happen. I am not going to argue about it; I am not going to dignify the accusations made by the hon. member with a reply. I stake my reputation in the province of Alberta and the city of Edmonton against those people, and I am quite prepared to let it rest that way. Time takes care of these things.
Elections do, too.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to get on with the estimates. I want to thank hon.

members for the consideration they have given the Department of Agriculture today in connection with the resolution on farm credit which farmers are very anxious to have and which they need, and also for the consideration given by many hon. members in connection with the debate on the supply motion the first two days of this week.
We are now dealing with the main estimates of the Department of Agriculture, and of course we are going along spending this amount of money. I would hope this afternoon that in view of the fact that we have been dealing with both the supplementary and main estimates for eight days this session- I believe this will be the ninth day-and that we do have two amendments to bills and a new machinery bill coming before the house in the next 30 days, hon. members will consider there will be a lot of time on these measures to have a full discussion on agriculture. There will be lots of time for a full discussion on agriculture on those matters, and possibly today we can get down to the details of the estimates of the department.

If the minister is not going
to dignify the statement I made by replying to it, will he at least tell members of the committee whether he intends to take any action with respect to the obvious conflict which exists between the affidavits of Mr. McKay and Mr. Trach?
I have nothing to add to what I have already said.
Then may I quote, sir-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has just made his speech, and we have heard from the Minister of Agriculture. We are still on the first item and the hon. member for Yukon will have an opportunity to make another contribution. I respectfully suggest we should give other members an opportunity to participate in the debate. With the co-operation of the committee I suggest that we call on the hon. member for Shefford.

Mr. Chairman, I thank you for giving me this opportunity to contribute to the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. There are certainly many things to be said when discussing our farming industry, and I shall limit my considerations more particularly to the problems of eastern farming.
A few days ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) told us that he intended to put an aircraft at the disposal of committee
Supply-Agriculture
members so as to enable them to visit the various provinces and see for themselves on the spot, what the farm problems are in each Canadian province. This suggestion will certainly please several committee members, and at least enable them to study new farm problems which have not yet been brought to their attention.
As far as we are concerned, in eastern Canada, we are quite familiar with farm problems, and when I think that the minister is putting an aircraft at the disposal of the committee on agriculture to make its members aware of farm problems in other provinces, I am reminded of the farmer who was taking a plane for the first time. When the plane was airborne, the farmer went to the washroom. Once there, he saw that there was a poster above the door: Do not use over towns and villages. And the farmer thought to himself: "We are the ones who will get that on the head".
Mr. Chairman, when I consider the agricultural policy, and especially the intentions which were put forward by the Conservatives, during the six years when they were in office-and I must state that several Conservative members said that their party intended to develop a feed grain policy in order to help the farmers of the province of Quebec, but that unfortunately they could not do it because they were defeated and a general election was held-I feel that we must ask the Liberal party to act as quickly as possible so that the Canadian agricultural policy will not be made only of good intentions but will also include achievements. In fact, we must remember that the road to hell is paved with good intentions, and parliament must not be the place where only good intentions are found, but also achievements.
When the Minister of Agriculture tells us that there are no more agricultural problems, that everything is fine, I have no alternative but to ask him a single question, to which I should like to have an answer. How can he explain that bird seed which, last year, was worth 14 cents a pound, cost now 42 cents? That means an increase of 200 per cent, for only one of the grains that the farmer must buy.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to support my remarks with some excerpts from the newspaper La Terre de Chez Nous, which is known as the official publication of the Catholic farmers' union of the province of Quebec, and especially of the French Canadian element in our agricultural class.

Supply-Agriculture
However, before that, I wish to pay special tribute to our Canadian farmers who, to date, have placed a plentiful production at our disposal. They produced eggs, milk, pork, butter, cheese, chicken and broilers in large quantities, as well as various vegetable products, and I feel we should recognize that fact and be proud of it. Indeed, if we profit today by such a varied and abundant farm production, we should be grateful to our farming population, which unsparingly works our soil, which is recognized as very fertile.
As for our farm production, I wish to quote an article which appeared in La Terre de Chez Nous on April 22, 1964. On page 24, we read this:
Plenty o 1 eggs and chickens.
During the first two months of 1964, egg production increased by 5 per cent as compared to the first two months of the previous year. The rate of laying had increased by 6 per cent on February 1 and by 3 per cent on March 1.
For the first two months of 1964, broiler chicken production remained higher than during the same period last year. For the second quarter of the current year (April-May-June), such production is likely to exceed by about 4 per cent that of the second quarter of 1963.
Turkey.
General prospects for 1964: weak to fair increase of numbers in relation to 1963. Up to now, there has been an increase of 5 per cent in incubation of young turkeys.
Turkey meat stocks increase continuously.
All this, Mr. Chairman, goes to show that our farm production increases constantly and that we should commend our Canadian farmers for it.
But on the other hand as our agricultural production increases, we must also consider what income our farmers are getting in Canada, in the province of Quebec and more particularly in eastern Canada.
We must take a look at the income that those farmers who produce so much and so well are getting as a return for their production. And on that matter, I refer once again to the newspaper La Terre de Chez Nous, and more particularly to page 11 of the May 6, 1964 issue:
Fifty per cent of Canadian farmers make less than $2,500 a year.
The proportion of Canadian farmers with an Income over $10,000 a year is only 10.4 per cent. But those who make up that 10 per cent own 23.4 per cent of farmed lands and provide 44.7 per cent of the whole farm production in our country.
That first group of 10.4 per cent is therefore by far the most important as regards agricultural production. That group is also the one which collects the best of government grants such as fixed acreage payments and summer fallow grants, two measures applied to date only In the prairie provinces.

Another group, which offers a striking contrast with the first one, is the group of farmers with a gross income of less than $2,500 a year. That second group involves about half of Canadian farmers.
Now, when you consider our plentiful production and at the same time the statistics and the official reports of the Catholic farmers' union a certain anomaly is brought to light.
At the same time the income of our agricultural people is very low but in the house, there does not seem to be any other way than to offer farm loans to our farmers and to get them more and more into debt.
Again, this morning, a resolution is being moved and in a few days a bill will be put before us to increase the Farm Credit Corporation's borrowing capacity so as to enable them to grant more loans.
The farmers' credit problem is not the only important one; there is also the problem of providing them with the necessary income, proportionate to their production, so that they will be able to meet their obligations concerning these loans. On page 20 of the April 29, 1964 issue of La Terre de Chez Nous, it was stated:
For the first time in the history of this organization, the total amount of loans exceeds $100 million.
According to the figures released by Mr. George Owen, president of the corporation, the total number of loans approved last year amounted to 8,689, for a value of $108,009,100.
In comparing these figures to the previous record of 7,438 loans and $90,924,300 for the fiscal year ended on the last day of March 1963, we find an increase of 16.8 per cent in the number and of 18.8 per cent in the total value of the loans.
Well, it is proposed to make more loans available to the farmers without worrying too much about a farm policy that would enable them to meet their obligations. The Porter commission has also examined the matter of farm loans and here is what it suggests.
I am in complete disagreement with what it suggests concerning farm loans. In one of its recommendations, the Porter commission is advocating the increase of the interest rate the federal Farm Credit Corporation is charging on its loans, that is, that the 5 per cent flat rate be raised to the prevailing rate on the market, which is about 6J per cent. And the commission recommends:
1.	The removal of the 5 per cent ceiling on the interest rate charged by the banks;
2.	The withdrawal of government guarantees as soon as the banks realize the loans are safe;
3.	The increase from $7,500 to $10,000 of the maximum amount of a farm improvement loan granted by a bank. The commissioners noted that the lending rate had remained at 5 per cent since

the Farm Improvement Loans Act was first put in operation 18 years ago.
The commissioners added:
We do not believe that the banks would reduce their lending to farmers if the general mortgage prohibition were removed and the banks were permitted to lend at approximate market rates of interest which would at times exceed the present 6 per cent limit. They might be prepared to lend more freely than at the present uneconomic 5 per cent rate.
Here we have the Porter commission suggesting that, in order to assist our Canadian farmers, the interest rate on farm loans should be raised. Then, they will wonder why it is that with an average income of $2,500 for 50 per cent of our farmers in Canada, with a farm loan which it is suggested to raise to $40,000 with an interest rate of 6J per cent, which will amount to some $2,600 in interest every year on the farm loan, that the farmer cannot meet his obligations. How can he meet them if our agricultural policy is not changed?
In La Terre de Chez Nous of April 15, 1964, page 3, we could read the following:
"Master of our own house". There is an almost ideal slogan for politicians. It could also be a very laudable and even a very sound objective, provided the necessary steps to reach it or at least to get closer and closer to it are taken.
For our farmers, we must recognize that such is not the case and that it is rather the contrary which is shaping up. Indeed, the farmer, because of a continually deteriorating situation and because of the failure of the leaders at the various levels to consider his lot, is less and less the master of his own business. You just have to think about vertical integration in agriculture with everything it implies and the various forms it takes, to realize that farmers are more and more at the mercy of enterprises whose interests are far from being the same as those of farmers, when they are not absolutely at variance.
Moreover, for all practical purposes, government authorities unfortunately ignore or forget altogether the problem of production credit. Indeed, there are certain forms of credit but they consist mostly in financing anew, at each generation, the farmer's property-
When we consider such basic problems as marketing and all related factors, we have the distinct feeling that some of the major officials of the department, who are supposed to look after farmers, consider with nostalgia and regret the disappearance of a regime which enabled them to grant farmers a few favours and to bring them to heel. In some cases, they do everything they can to prevent the regime from dying out.
For the time being, we would like to quote from a speech delivered recently by a former Nova Scotia deputy minister of agriculture which shows that we should open our eyes a little to find out what is happening outside our province before beaming complacently over our situation and our achievements. I quote: "Marketing, said the guest speaker, is the key to farm prosperity. Not production or anything else, but marketing. The speaker also immediately added that, for 20220-238
The late Mr. S. H. Rideout
rather strange reasons, many provincial governments and the government at Ottawa preferred to turn their backs on marketing. They are instead placing more emphasis on the production and the efficiency of those they are calling "production guys'. Such a policy may have its good points, said Mr. Walsh, but it cannot solve the farm problem because the farmer produces everything in abundance and very efficiently." A conclusion is obvious at this time: unless there is a radical change in the concept of the role of the various people responsible for the fate of our agriculture and unless that is truly translated into practice, in spite of the general aim proclaimed for the province, "Masters in our own house", the farmers of Quebec will become more and more "Slaves in their own house".
Mr. Chairman, may I call it one o'clock?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE LATE SHERWOOD H. RIDEOUT TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with sadness that, on behalf of the Prime Minister, I rise to speak of one of our number who passed away suddenly this morning at eleven o'clock as he proceeded on the Ocean Limited to Moncton in his constituency. I am sure that all members of this house share with me a deep sense of sorrow at the loss of one of our members from New Brunswick, Sherwood Hayes Rideout, the member for Westmorland.
Mr. Rideout was one of the younger and active members of this house. He was born in 1917. During his life he gave much to the public life of his community, his province and to Canada. Certainly, as a member of this house he served his constituents industriously and with sincerity. Mr. Rideout served as a trainmaster on the Canadian National Railways in his home community, and as such he had a special interest in transportation and trade problems of the Atlantic provinces. He was an active member of local 162 of the brotherhood of locomotive engineers. He served as an alderman in his city for two terms and became mayor of Moncton in 1961,

He served them officially and unofficially, and he served organizations such as the mental health association and the retarded children's association. The men who saved the world are those who work by rule of thumb; who do the day's work by the day's light and advance on chaos and the painful dark by inches; in other words, the practical men.
To his family, his wife and his three sons, I extend the sincere sympathy of the Prime Minister, the members of the government and the membership of this house. A good man has left us, but he has left a rich memory of devoted service to his people and to his nation.

Although he was only 47 years of age he already had a very considerable life of public service to his credit. He had acted on the county council, on the school board, had been an alderman and more recently mayor of the city of Moncton, and he was a member of this parliament. This is a very enviable public record for a man only 47 years of age, and those of us who had the privilege of meeting him since he came to Ottawa were impressed with his friendliness and convinced that his career held great promise for the future. Now he has been cut off at this early age, and I am sure all of us feel a great sense of regret and loss.
The members of this party would like to extend to the government and all its supporters, to Mrs. Rideout and the members of the family, and to his constituents in Westmorland, our deepest sympathy at the great loss which they have sustained this day.

It may not be well known to the members of this house, but the city of Moncton and the city of Medicine Hat were twinned for the centennial celebrations which are to take place in 1967. During the past few weeks and days the hon. member and I had discussed on many occasions some of the things which we could do as members

of parliament to bring about an intermingling of the citizens of these two cities with a view to strengthening the understanding between the various regions of this country. We had decided that we were going to exchange positions for a day or for a week so that we could learn about each other's constituencies. One of the special reasons for twinning the city of Medicine Hat with the city of Moncton was because of the large French speaking population in that city.
Canada has lost a great citizen, Mr. Speaker, a citizen who could look beneath the surface and who could look into the future and try to work out some of those problems which we as a nation have. I want to say on behalf of the leader of this party and all of the members of this party that we have a very deep sense of sympathy at this time for his family.

Mr. Chairman, before

of the chamber when I say, as our leader has said, that we shall miss him very much.
I want to assure the minister that there is no desire on the part of the members of this party to delay unduly the passing of his estimates. However, at the same time I am sure he will realize that we have an obligation and a responsibility as members of parliament to offer our suggestions and indeed our criticisms as well as subjecting the estimates of his department to that careful examination that is required of us at these times. The minister mentioned that we had already spent nine days on the estimates and I think this impression should be corrected. He lumped in the supplementary estimates with the main estimates. Of course we all recall what happened during the course of the debate on the supplementary estimates. I think the minister knows full well that had they come clean with us at that time, had they answered the fears that we expressed during the course of that debate, the estimates would have passed in considerably less time than they did. As it turned out, the examination that was carried on under the auspices of the Minister fo Justice revealed without any doubt at all that there was some question as to the legality of the actions that were taken during the period when there was a transfer of responsibilities; and the fact that a special order in council had to be passed to ratify the actions that had been taken was, to us, sufficient justification for the prolonged debate at that time. Our experience, also, has been that any estimates or policies of this government require careful examination.
During the introduction of the minister's estimates to the committee he dwelt at some length on the work that has been done in so far as production research is concerned. Certainly we on this side of the chamber are well aware of the need for production research, efforts to reduce the costs of production and to provide better varieties of crops suitable to the growing conditions that exist here in Canada. But he said nothing about a matter that we feel is very much related to the question of production research, and that is marketing research. To proceed apace with production research without carrying on the kind of marketing research that is necessary to dispose of the increased production that will result is simply asking the farmers to run faster but to stay in the same place. I would suggest to the minister, in keeping with the promises the Liberal party made during the election campaign, that some con-

siderable effort needs to be spent on the question of marketing research, and I would like to hear him say something about that matter as we proceed with the estimates.
He also quoted with some relish the cash income figures for agriculture during the past year. Admittedly the cash income figures look very appealing, but 1 cannot understand the reluctance on the part of the government in power to quote the figures that really mean something to the farmer; that is, the realized net income figures. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle put those figures on the record the other day and I have no intention of repeating them. However, they certainly do reveal that all is not as well as the government proclaims. No matter how good the cash income figures for Canada may look, my experience has been that there are always areas, always pockets where all is not so well. To quote these figures without giving consideration to the areas that are in difficulty is like suggesting that a man with one foot in a bucket of ice and the other one on a hot plate is, on the average, very comfortable. I am sure no one will agree that this is the ultimate in comfort.
The minister suggested, also-and I was rather interested in this remark-that the farmer's image, as far as the urban populations of Canada are concerned, has been somewhat tarnished, and he referred to a conversation he had with someone in Toronto when he said, "How do you like all that money we sent you to keep you on the farm?", referring to the western farmer. He said something might be done about this. I would suggest that the minister can do something by telling the Liberal candidates in the next election campaign that when they are campaigning in their ridings they should not exaggerate and falsify the figures and should not say that the Conservative government had to be turned out simply because they were doing too much for the farmer. I think that to a large extent this is the reason for that tarnished image. I am not blaming the minister for this, but I hope he will bring together some of the members of his party and call them to task for the misinformation they spread during the last two election campaigns.
The minister made some comment about dairy policy. This has been dealt with at some length by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska and I do not intend to go into that matter. But I think the minister should remember that the dairy industry is a com-

plex one and the figures relating to that
industry as a whole can be somewhat misleading, because there are four component parts of the dairy industry. I am quite convinced they are not all enjoying the degree of prosperity which he indicated. He took great pains to point out the policies he had initiated since he took office, and said they were responsible for the success which he alleges the dairy industry is enjoying. None of us on this side is going to be fooled by those comments. We know the dairy policy he has followed is the policy that was initiated by the previous government through the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
If the minister wants a complete solution to the dairy problem I would suggest he should pursue that very same policy whereby the four components of the dairy industry -the fluid milk producers, the concentrated milk shippers, the men who ship milk to the cheese factories, and the cream suppliers- can all have the same opportunity to enjoy the same degree of prosperity.
On occasion when listening to the minister I have come to the conclusion that his idea of Utopia in agriculture will be when millionaires and industrialists purchase all the smaller farms in the country and operate them, as was the case under the feudal system. I hope this is not his philosophy, but sometimes I wonder when I listen to his remarks.
During the past few weeks we heard a great deal about solemn commitments and how important it is to implement the commitments made during the election campaigns. Mr. Chairman, quite a number of solemn commitments with respect to agriculture were made by the Liberal party during the last two elections, and it might be well to put a few of them on the record and find out how many have been implemented.
Surely a commitment to a farmer is as valid as a commitment to anyone in any other segment of industry. Surely the government has not completely forgotten some of the promises it made during the course of the last two campaigns. I have in my hand a pamphlet which I had some difficulty locating. It is entitled, "A Square Deal for Farmers," and I could not locate it until I looked under the file marked "fiction." Some of the promises contained in it are startling in view of the results achieved thus far.
First of all, the Liberal government was going to expand Canada's exports of farm products. I would like to hear from the minister in what way exports were expanded, other than simply following the patterns and

policies laid down by the previous government, except for some modifications and changes which I am not criticizing because, in the light of changing conditions, perhaps they were necessary. I would like to know what specific effort has been made to encourage exports of Candaian farm products.
The Liberal party said it was going to serve farmers with information on the market outlook, but I happen to recall that not long ago in this chamber the Minister of Transport, who in those days acted as agricultural critic, took the former minister of agriculture to task for spending money for that precise purpose. He was in disagreement with any effort to pass on to farmers information that was important to them in the planning of their production, and information regarding the market possibilities for their products. I do not recall the particular date or year, but I do remember the date. The Minister of Transport is not in the chamber today, but I am sure he could remind members of his party when that debate took place.
Another item in this pamphlet states they would improve consultation about farm policies. I wonder in what way has consultation been improved. Only the other day the minister had an appointment with leaders of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I think it was on Tuesday, May 19, and the appointment had been made some time previously, but an hour before the delegation was to arrive in Ottawa they received a phone call to say the minister could not see them. He had gone out west to speak to a Kiwanis club.
What date was this, because I spent a whole day with the federation of agriculture?
This was Tuesday the 19th.
The 19th of what month?
Of this month.
This is not correct.

I will be glad to be corrected if I have misrepresented the facts, but this was my information and if the minister wants to put the record straight, well, fine, that is all right with me.
Another one of the policies which the Liberal party said it would implement was the establishment of an independent research council for marketing, processing and production. At the time this promise was made there had already been an independent research council set up under the responsibility of the minister of agriculture for the province of Manitoba, Hon. George Hutton.
