Perhaps the minister would care to outline how an independent research council, sponsored and paid for by the government, can be independent. The independence of the council that is in existence today certainly cannot be questioned, but I doubt very much if such a council paid for, set up and appointed by the government, can exercise any degree of independence whatsoever.
The pamphlet went on to say they were going to provide long term capital for cooperatives through the industrial development bank. I have not seen anything of this. They were also going to encourage the establishment of marketing boards where farmers wanted them. Mr. Chairman, marketing boards can be established in any of the provinces any time the farmers wish to do so. This pamphlet is only a lot of useless words, trying to gild the lily a little bit, but meaningless, as were most of the Liberal promises during the election campaigns.
They said they would improve price support measures. I would like to know in what way they have done so. I know the Liberal candidate in the Provencher riding carried on his own election campaign, and I suppose this was true of most Liberal candidates across the country. The federal Liberal party had one policy and the candidates followed another.
I have in my hand a full page ad that appeared in my local newspaper, in which the Liberal candidate for Provencher started out by saying that if the people wanted these things they must vote for him for strong, stable, responsible government. I do not think I need to comment on the stable aspects of this government. These are well known. The candidate also promised deficiency payments to cream shippers, to eggs and pork producers, paid on a regional and quarterly basis. I wonder where that promise has gone. Then he went on to promise higher initial payments for wheat, oats and barley, announced before seeding time. Have we heard anything about that? Then he promised a guaranteed scale of price supports on wheat, oats and barley, for example, with a minimum guaranteed price of $2 for No. 1 wheat. That is another promise that has gone by the wayside. Then for No. 2 wheat, he says, $1.99 and for No. 3, $1.98. He is taking it upon himself to set the spread between Nos. 1, 2 and 3 wheat and anyone who knows anything about wheat marketing in this country knows that these spreads of one cent between each grade are about the most ludicrous thing we have ever seen. Finally, he says: "For a two

price system on wheat calculated on the unit quota".
Well, we have heard the last of that, no doubt. This is set out in somewhat less detail in the pamphlet. They were going to provide deficiency payments for grain, which includes, I suppose, the program announced by the Liberal candidate in Provencher and then, by a consumer subsidy, improve the return to farmers on wheat consumed by Canadians. That is a general statement and I do not think anyone knows what it means. We certainly have not seen any results. Then, they state, they would underwrite provincial crop insurance programs. I presume the intention is to introduce a system of re-insurance such as that proposed by the government of Manitoba, who have been leaders in the field of provincial crop insurance programs. As most members are aware, the legislation we passed as to crop insurance was enabling legislation providing for some assistance to provincial governments which adopted a system of crop insurance in their respective provinces, and the province of Manitoba has enlarged this program now to the point where more than 6,200 farmers are covered, as compared with about 5,100 last year. So this program is expanding and they are prepared to expand it still further as soon as this government is prepared, as was indicated in this election speech, to implement this promise about re-insurance as requested by the Manitoba government. They said they were willing to improve farm credit and we are glad to see that the bill respecting this has been given first reading and that it is likely to become a reality soon. Then they go on to say:
By area development programs, and with the necessary capital, improve farm land, turn submarginal land to more profitable uses, draw new sources of jobs to rural areas, and improve educational and training opportunities.
Surely they do not think they are fooling anybody with this gobbledygook. They know full well that these are the objectives laid down in ARDA. All they are suggesting here is that they intend to carry on the ARDA program and I do not need to tell members of this house or anyone in the country who introduced that program.
Then it says: "Undertake a program of water conservation". That also has been carried on for years under P.F.R.A. and it is also a part of the ARDA program. Speaking of water conservation, I should be happy if the minister would take another look at the Morris dam in my riding. I should be very happy if the minister could convince treasury

board that this project is one of the necessary water conservation projects for the province of Manitoba.
Then, I suppose in order to fill up the page, they say they intend to carry on all these policies in co-operation with the provinces. I suppose that is a departure from what they have been doing under the various programs they have introduced so far. But we are happy to see they intend to co-operate with the provinces in the field of agriculture, at least. The parliamentary secretary, who is listening to my remarks intently, emphasized when he spoke the other day on a supply motion the amount of production research which is being carried on under the government and he left the impression that this was something new-something which had been initiated by this government. I cannot let such an impression be given without making some comment, because surely the hon. gentleman should know that production research has been carried on ever since there have been experimental farms in Canada. There can be no question but that the production research which has been carried on under successive governments has been a credit to the Department of Agriculture. However, he sought to leave the impression- I think, a superfluous one-that new vistas of opportunity were suddenly to be opened up to the farmers simply because they were carrying on this production research.
I was interested in the comment made here the other day by the hon. member for Kings, who seemed to be most impressed with the fact that the Department of Agriculture had been divided up so badly. He seemed to think this would lead to all kinds of co-operation and that great things were to be done as a result of this division. We do not know who is actually in charge of the department because the other day when the hon. member for the Yukon brought some matters to the attention of the government there were a number who took part in the debate, including the Prime Minister, the Minister of Forestry, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Industry. They all pitched in and joined in the act. I wonder how they can reconcile their philosophy and approach in the Department of National Defence, the achievement of unification there, with the divisions which are taking place within the Department of Agriculture. In one instance we are told of a wonderful new move to have everything unified in one camp, while in another department the best thing which could hap-
Supply-Agriculture
pen, if we are to believe the hon. members opposite, is to split the administration up. I contend there can be no effective co-operation in the face of the division of responsibility which now exists in the Department of Agriculture. The hon. member for Kings went on to say-
On a point of order, I am not bilingual and there is a battle going on in the other official language in one corner of the chamber. I cannot take in the two languages at the same time.

He seemed to find in these divisions the ultimate solution, but as far as the government is concerned, it has led to a ludicrous situation. They want two ministers of agriculture. We have been supplied, so far, with four pension plans; we have two flags, and they have two policies for the tobacco industry, one to discourage the use of tobacco and another to encourage the use of tobacco. If that is their idea of unification and co-operation, if that is how they intend to run the department, I begin to feel sorry about what is going to happen.
The hon. member for Kings went on to tell us that the minister had made a well received statement to the federation of agriculture in Charlottetown. We know the minister has a good deal of personal charm. There is no question but that he enthralled his audience. But I can hardly concur with the conclusion drawn by the hon. member that this one speech to the federation of agriculture suddenly resolved all the difficulties of agriculture.
There is one thing I should like to put on the record. The other day the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska put some figures on record relating to feed prices in his area and the fluctuations in those prices from month to month. I thought they were interesting because the hon. member for Kings, the parliamentary secretary, the minister himself and other speakers on this subject have drawn the conclusion, prematurely I think, that stability had finally been brought to the industry in eastern Canada. Well, the fluctuations which took place between August of last year and April of this year certainly indicate that this stability does not exist. I say this because there was a fluctuation between the low and the high of 75 cents a hundredweight.
I went to the trouble of communicating with the accounts division to find out what were the particular prices allocated on a monthly basis for these same months. I find

Supply-Agriculture
a variation in prices during that same period, from a high to a low, of 16 cents per bushel. If you want to relate this to the hundredweight, it amounts to about 24.6 cents. The price to the producer in western Canada varied by about 24.6 cents per hundred and the price to the consumer in eastern Canada varied as much as 75 cents per hundred. Surely, in the face of figures such as those no one could claim that ultimate stability has been created. I ask the minister to take a second look at the program he has instituted and not be so complacent about how successful it has been.
In the case of oats, the variation to the consumer is about 28 cents a bushel, compared to a variation of 26 cents a bushel in the wheat board average price at the lake-head. This was approximately 60 cents per hundred. In the case of barley, the variation is 37 cents as compared with a variation of 8 cents a bushel or 16 cents a hundredweight in the wheat board price. I have these figures in table form. I do not want to take the time of the committee to put them on the record, but I am sure the committee would be interested in having these figures put on Hansard as part of my speech. I ask if this course is agreeable to the committee?
Could we have them read into the record?

Do you want them read into the record? I have put on the record the important parts. The variations in monthly prices in eastern Canada were put on the record by the hon. member for Nicolet-Ya-maska; I do not think it is necessary for me to put them on the record again. I choose not to read them into the record. As a matter of fact, I intend to give them to the press if they want to use them. I know what members opposite are attempting to do. They want to restrict my speech by having me read these figures into the record, but I do not intend to accommodate them. I have a few minutes left and I intend to devote that time to other matters.
The minister certainly cannot conclude that the policy he adopted of paying the storage charges on grain in store in eastern Canada has in any way whatever created that degree of stability that he tries to leave the impression has been created in feed mill prices in eastern Canada. I ask him to continue looking into this situation and to pursue a more aggressive policy in order to ensure that there is real stability in feed prices in eastern Canada. This is a problem for the eastern

farmer, and will continue to be a problem until some effective action has been taken.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order; I must advise the hon. member that the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity this afternoon of taking part briefly in the debate on agriculture. I believe the fact that so many days have been spent on agriculture is an indication of the importance which this item holds for all members of the house. We have had a general debate on agriculture. In addition, we have had a discussion with regard to the problems of eastern agriculture. It may be that many of us are not aware of the fact that agriculture does hold a very important place in the province from which I come, the province of British Columbia. It is true that the arable land area in British Columbia is very limited. I believe the maximum would be about 4 per cent of the land area at the present time.
In spite of that fact, it is a very important industry so far as British Columbia is concerned. In so far as my own constituency of Fraser Valley is concerned, it is most assuredly one of the major industries of that particular section of British Columbia. I have the British Columbia News Letter for July, 1963, in which there is a reference to the cash income of British Columbia farmers. This is broken down by major commodities produced by the British Columbia farmer in 1962. It is pointed out that dairy products account for about $36 million; cattle and calves, $30.4 million; fruit, $19.4 million; eggs, $15.3 million; poultry, $12.2 million; vegetables and potatoes, $10.2 million and wheat, $3.7 million. I believe these figures indicate as I have pointed out before, that agriculture is an important part of the economy of British Columbia.
In a brief presented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the Prime Minister of Canada and members of the cabinet on February 26, 1964, there are several observations made in respect of farming in general. They agree that they are possibly taking a new approach in the presentation of an agricultural brief and point out, for instance, that as an industry agriculture has been and remains, in spite of whatever necessary measures have been taken to improve its position, the most vulnerable and relatively unprotected industrial sector in the country. I feel this is one of the things that has been a matter of great concern to the people engaged in agriculture. It certainly has occupied the time and

the attention of the organizations representing agriculture. They have pointed out time and time again that while the costs of production are increasing, there is very little protection so far as the farmer is concerned of the prices he receives for his products. This, of course, places him in a very difficult financial position.
The brief also points out that, as a group, the farmers have shared less in the post-war period in the rising levels of wealth and income than any other group in the country. I think that the statistics that are presented from time to time will show this is very true. The brief points out also that the expenditures in agriculture are taken up pretty well in increasing the quality and abundance of food which has been sold at lower prices. It also refers to agriculture assistance. I believe the hon. member for Provencher referred to this when he called attention to the criticism that is levelled sometimes against the agriculture segment of our economy because of the subsidies or the assistance that is granted in various forms.
While there have been times when it almost seemed as though there were substantial amounts of money being put into this particular phase, I think that, in the over-all picture, the assistance has been very modest. Furthermore, it is justified in view of the particular problems that agriculture faces. I am sure we are all aware of the necessity for agriculture production. We are dependant upon agriculture for our sustenance. I believe, therefore, that in the consideration of the problems that agriculture faces we should be thinking that any assistance we give in this connection is worth while in that it maintains production for Canadian consumption.
Another factor mentioned is that agriculture is a vital sector of the health of the economy; and I think it has been said many times that as agriculture prospers so the economy prospers. I think that is true. Another factor pointed out by the brief is that among advanced nations Canada spends a relatively small proportion of the national budget on agriculture, and I believe this as well is borne out by statistics.
Coming to the problems of British Columbia and especially of my own riding, I should like to say that I have had a number of communications from those engaged in the industry and also those who are representative of the industry in the province of British Columbia. One of the main points of concern is the effect of possible tariff changes as they relate to agricultural production. The British Columbia coast vegetable marketing
Supply-Agriculture
board, representing a great number of organizations, have submitted material for consideration, and perhaps it would be interesting to record the participating organizations associated with this particular submission. They are as follows: Abbotsford growers co-op association; B.C. coast vegetable marketing board; B.C. coast vegetable co-operative association; B.C. interior vegetable marketing board; B.C. interior marketing agency limited; B.C. blueberry co-operative association limited; B.C. certified seed potato growers association; B.C. lower mainland farmers' co-operative association; Columbia potato growers association; Colebrook potato growers association; district "E" farmers' institute of B.C.; East Chilliwack co-operative growers; Fraser valley fruit and vegetable growers association; Fraser valley pea growers association; Fresh-Pak Limited, Burnaby (processors); Georgia potato growers association; lower B.C. mainland horticultural association; Pacific co-operative union (growers); south Vancouver island potato growers association; united flower growers co-operative association; united Fraser valley growers co-operative association, and the Vancouver island vegetable co-operative association.
This indicates, Mr. Chairman, that this brief and the fears expressed therein is representative of the great many organizations, and of course producers, in these various areas of activity. I should like to read a short paragraph from page 2 of the brief. It is pointed out that:
We, as producers in B.C., with a minimum ot tariff protection now available are able to supply other western provinces with early crop vegetables and various small fruits. We firmly believe that it is to the benefit of our producers, consumers, distributors and processors and the economy of our country to further foster this ever increasing movement within our Canadian regions rather than have these markets supplied by imported produce which we believe would completely dominate our Canadian markets under any method of reduced tariff protection.
It is pointed out in this particular brief that prior to 1959, I believe it is, the producers in that area were severely handicapped owing to the importation of fruits and vegetables from across the border. The producers there had the best of the market in their own country, and then just before our own producers put their produce on the market it was flooded with what was left over from south of the border. Then certain changes were effected which placed them in a more competitive position and I believe added greatly to the stability of the fruit

Supply-A griculture
and vegetable industries in the province of British Columbia. The fear is that in the event that certain proposed changes are made and tariffs are reduced, our producers will once again be faced with this very same problem. They are voicing great concern and asking that in any negotiations which are carried on between Canada and other nations of the world under GATT or the Kennedy round, as the present negotiations are called, or any type of negotiations, some of these basic considerations will be borne in mind and that nothing will be done to jeopardize the position of our industries in the province of British Columbia. I think this is fundamental. I think it is basic. I believe it is only fair, because if our own producers lose the position they have now and the market is supplied from outside, our own industries may be put out of operation and prices could rise to the point where we would wish we had our own producers producing our own foodstuffs for us.
There are many problems faced by those engaged in agriculture. As I have said, those in my own riding also have their own particular problems and have to face the situation with a great deal of courage, realizing that there are so many things which could happen to interfere with the satisfactory production and distribution of their products. I just call these matters to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture.
There is one other matter I should like to mention at this time. Some time ago the question was raised as to protection for agricultural producers under the Bankruptcy Act. There have been cases where producers who are farmers have delivered their produce to companies which have subsequently been declared bankrupt. Under the terms of the act no provision is made to reimburse farmers or to enable them to make a claim. Therefore they are requesting that the act be amended so that these people will receive protection, and in the event of such a thing happening will not be in the position of losing their entire crop or their entire production.
I do not propose, Mr. Chairman, to discuss agricultural matters any further at this time. I realize there is a desire on the part of the committee to facilitate the passage of the estimates in view of the fact that we have spent considerable time on them. May I again say that this is only an indication of the fact that we are all interested in and concerned about the problems of agriculture in our own areas as well as right across the nation, and we trust that these matters which are brought

to the attention of the minister from time to time will be given every consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to dwell unduly long this afternoon on the subject with which we are dealing. I would like to extend to the members of the government, to his colleagues on the other side of the aisle and to his wife and family who survive him, my deep condolences upon the death of Sherwood Rideout, the hon. member for Westmorland.
My remarks this afternoon will deal primarily with the dairy industry, and principally with the cheese segment of that industry. I will also have a few words to say about ARDA and some of its facets, and in a limited way, regarding farm credit.
Beginning with the cheese industry, Mr. Chairman, I wish to point out that the farmers of Ontario and the Ontario cheese producers marketing board, which works in their interests, were very disappointed with the recent announcement of the Minister of Agriculture on Thursday, May 14, cutting cheese export assistance by another cent. As you know, Mr. Chairman, the assistance in the amount of four cents a pound, so wisely and beneficially established by the Conservative administration, has now been cut exactly in half so that whatever benefits the cheese producers receive are of very little consequence to such a vital industry engaged in exporting Canada's principal specialty product.
I reiterate that Canadian cheddar cheese is Canada's principal specialty export product. Canada has other products, of course, that are specialties of our nation. I am not taking anything away from Canadian maple syrup or No. 1 northern hard wheat; but of all the products that Canada exports to the old country cheese seems to be the leader, so far as the tastes of the British consumers are concerned. Therefore the action of the government, the Department of Agriculture and the man heading that department has been retrogressive with respect to the progress that the cheese industry must and should make.
Is it not true that the minister was asked by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the dairy farmers of Canada, the Ontario cheese producers, the L and S co-operative and the Lake St. John co-operative, representing the Quebec cheese producers, to continue the three cent subsidy on export cheese? In spite of that the minister left these people in the lurch and cut the export assistance by another cent. From whom did the minister take his advice when he lowered the subsidy on export cheese from four to two cents?

Did he take the advice of the butter and milk powder interests?
Is it right, with this reduction of one cent in the assistance for export cheese, that farmers all across Canada should have to take a reduction of nine or ten cents per 100 pounds for their milk? That is what the mathematics of the matter will mean unless it is possible to raise the price of Canadian cheese one cent per pound on the United Kingdom market. It would be a very ill-advised thing to raise the price on that market because this year we must export a great deal more than last to take care of the reduction in the subsidy, and the contemplated increase in production of cheese-milk.
The price of Canadian cheese on the United Kingdom market has already been raised four cents in a two year period compared with an increase of one and a half cents in the price of New Zealand cheese in a four year period. Our Canadian cheese costs the English importer 37 cents a pound laid down in London compared with 32J cents a pound for New Zealand cheese properly aged for consumption. Remember that the United Kingdom importer has to keep Canadian cheese approximately one year for aging purposes whereas it seems that New Zealand cheese is already aged when it arrives in England.
Does the minister think it wise to increase our price in that market by another cent? We could well ruin our market there by too high a price and by always asking more and more for the product each time a shipment arrives in England. This latter is not good business. I have here the statement that the minister made in the house on May 14. As found on page 3255 of Hansard he said:
-so it is now considered in the best interests of all that this subsidy should be reduced by a further one cent per pound.
When the minister says "in the best interests of all" what does he mean? Does he mean the cheese industry, which is mostly farmer owned, or does he mean the butter and milk powder industries which are controlled by large corporations? I leave that question with members of this committee, Mr. Chairman, because it has not been answered and it is most vital to the progress of the cheese industry.
While I may be slightly out of order, Mr. Chairman, in passing I should like to point out the great discrepancy in the methods of taxing the various kinds of cheese companies. First, let me take the limited cheese company factory tax, which includes income
Supply-Agriculture
taxes and so on. A good example is the Elm-brook Cheese and Butter Manufacturing Company of Picton, Ontario, in Prince Edward county. That company has to struggle along paying as much as $1,200 a year in income taxes whereas a nearby co-operative manufacturing cheese pays no income tax. I am sure you will allow me to point that out to the house, Mr. Chairman. This situation is not the fault of the Department of Agriculture but it certainly represents a handicap to the limited companies which manufacture cheese in Canada today, and should be corrected.
There are a couple of other points I want to make on the question of the cheese export subsidy. The reduction of one cent per pound on export cheese will mean a reduction of nine or ten cents a hundred pounds on cheese milk to Canadian farmers, unless the price of cheese is increased in the United Kingdom market. We feel that such a move is unsound. Second, unless the export price of cheese can be raised to offset the one cent reduction by the federal government, the farmers of Canada are due to lose $1,370,000 on the basis of the production of 137 million pounds in 1963. The government of Canada has saved some $280,000 by reducing the export subsidy by one cent on 28 million pounds exported.
Officials of the government are predicting an increase of ten million pounds in cheese production in 1964. Are they asking this small group of farmers in the province of Ontario, who increased exports by ten million pounds in 1963, to increase them by another ten million pounds this year at a higher price? This does not look right, when the big companies that own whole milk powder plants are subsidized to the extent of 6.3 cents. I hope the minister realizes that this action simply represents a betrayal of the cheese milk producers by the government. I should like to see him rectify the situation soon in order to get that section of the dairy industry back on the track.
To turn to ARDA, although the government claims that it has made some progress and has put certain policies into effect, one can travel across the province of Ontario and see that it has done nothing by way of improvements under ARDA. ARDA has three main aims: to put to better use some marginal land that is not very productive in its present use-and nothing is being done along those lines outside of some pilot projects- second, ARDA is meant to develop income and employment opportunities in rural areas;

Supply-Agriculture
third, to develop and conserve the water and soil resources of rural Canada. I submit that this government has done nothing along these lines.
I do wish to remind the committee, Mr. Chairman, of the very able work performed by the hon. gentlemen in the other place. I have in my hand a report issued by a committee of the Senate, and having read most of it I want to compliment those hon. gentlemen in the red chamber for their able compilation of this report. I refer to the recent report of the special committee on land use in Canada. When the government and some political parties in this chamber are loudly contemplating and voting for the abolition of the other place, good work of this sort should remind them of the folly of such a measure. I want to quote from this report what the committee has to say about water and land use:
Water occupies a very influential role in determining the most beneficial use of land. Because of this, various witnesses devoted a part of their submissions to expressing a need for more concern about the use of this resource. The briefs pointed out that most uses of land require water. Despite this, the value of water is often overlooked. This lack will have to be remedied, especially in the areas where the limitations of water are becoming apparent. Less pollution and squandering of water will have to result, it was noted.
Here is the key point:
Decreasing water supplies in relative or absolute amounts create limitations to urban, industrial and recreational development, it was stated. Large quantities of water of suitable quality are required for these land uses.
Of particular concern to the committee was the role of water in agriculture. In eastern Canada many lands have the problem of too much water. Drainage must be provided for many agricultural lands. All levels of government are active in drainage programs. Many details were reported to the committee of the various schemes that are in operation to assist farmers in draining farming areas.
This is my point in this connection, Mr. Chairman. If this government really wishes to give leadership and guidance to the farmers of Canada, particularly those of eastern Canada, they should bend their efforts toward providing assistance to farmers wishing to instal tile drainage. I have here a copy of a resolution submitted to me over a month ago, but this is the first opportunity I have had to bring it to the attention of the government and hon. members. It is a copy of a resolution submitted by the Lennox and Addington county federation of agriculture regarding assistance that could be given to

farm drainage projects. I quote the resolution:
Whereas the present depreciation on farm installed tile drainage systems is now 2J per cent
And whereas at this rate, it would take 40 years to recover this cost
And whereas tile drainage is necessary in modem day agriculture
And is the first consideration in good farm management
And whereas this farm practice of tile drainage installation should be encouraged to a greater degree.
Therefore, be it resolved that the Lennox and Addington federation of agriculture request the Department of National Revenue taxation division to increase the capital cost allowance on already installed tile drainage systems from the present allowable 2J per cent to 10 per cent.
You will agree that this resolution is very valuable to the agricultural industry and its recommendation should be put into effect. I urge the government to think along those lines and see what they can do to assist the agricultural industry where tile drainage is required and farmers are loath to start on any large projects because of the small benefit that is granted taxwise.
My last point, Mr. Chairman, concerns farm credit and I wish to quote from that respected old journal, the Family Herald of May 21, 1964. This is the 95th year of publication of this magazine, which is very well known across Canada. In fact I can well remember running out to the mail box on the farm as a child once a week to get the Family Herald, which at that time was one of the main news media for rural Ontario. The article in this magazine is headed, "A crisis in farm credit" and it reads in part:
Though most Canadians find their weekly grocery bill a heavy burden to bear, they eat as well as any other nation on earth and a good deal cheaper than most. Their thanks for this blessing should be directed to the Canadian agricultural industry, a group of small, independent farmers producing a tremendous volume of food with a slim profit margin.
The article continues by referring to a well informed authority on real estate in western Canada, a person with a farm background, saying:
-that for his area, Farm Credit Corporation land value appraisals are out of date by at least ten years. "Farm Credit Corporation limits of $50,000 with terms of 35 to 50 years at no more than 3 per cent would be more realistic", he says, "even if it took two generations to pay it back".
I think we should be thinking along those lines, Mr. Chairman, with regard to lending money to prospective, young farmers who want to get into this industry. The article continues:

A charge frequently made Is that Farm Credit Corporation money is inflating farmland prices.
If that is so, it is making it all the more difficult for young people to get into the business. Then the article says:
Financing land purchases for increased efficiency is perhaps the farmer's biggest problem but close behind looms the problem of paying for basic and specialized machinery.
Many hon. members are farmers and know how difficult it is to finance machinery, where tremendous costs are involved, and pay mortgage interest and payments on their land, and so forth. I think it is time that we are looking into the loosening up and the expanding of the terms of these Farm Credit Corporation mortgages. To conclude the quotation:
It is frequently reported that the annual sums allotted by parliament to cover F.I.L. borrowing are never over-expended. Estimates of money actually borrowed vary and stood at around 60 per cent in a recent year. The repayment record on these funds is excellent. Where, then, is the bottleneck? Why are these funds not fully subscribed?
This is a question for which we are all responsible, but more particularly the government of the day. I hope it will look into this so that the agricultural industry can be put back on its financial feet. Our prime responsibility to this country is the working of the millions of acres of the top six inches of the soil of Canada.

I should first like to join with my fellow members and the leader of the official opposition in paying tribute to the late hon. member for Westmorland and in offering my condolences to the loved ones he has left behind.
While the minister may complain that this debate has dragged on, much of the time has been spent pointing out the evils of political patronage in the government, and it may be that not enough time has been spent on this important segment of our economy. Agriculture is still the biggest employer in Canada and is still the main industry of the country. This was admitted by the Minister of Finance on bringing down his budget this year. It was also pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, at various times throughout the year, that wheat sales and the agricultural economy itself brought buoyancy to our foreign exchange and improved economic conditions which were felt all across the country.
But is seems the government is more concerned with images than it is with agriculture, with this great economic lifeblood of Canada. From time to time we see the Prime Minister
Supply-Agriculture
worried about his own image and cancelling television programs. We see the Minister of Agriculture trying to portray his image across Canada as a robust auctioneer who has the small farmer's concern at heart, and who is bringing down four pieces of legislation which will vastly revolutionize farming. Why has he not brought them down? Why have we not had a look at them? Only one with regard to farm credit is on the order paper.
In a speech which he made in Lethbridge on April 30 he tried to give the impression that the opposition was doing nothing but filibustering. What legislation has come before parliament this session? We have had the speech from the throne and we spent six days of what might be termed our own time, during the Easter holidays, trying to proceed with government work. Certainly it cannot be said that those six days were taking up government time.
The minister said in Lethbridge on April 11:
The government legislation program is bogged down by opposition filibuster.
Where is this legislation that he wants to bring down to revolutionize farming? We see one item on the order paper and we have asked for it to be presented in bill form. The minister says some parliamentary rules and procedures could be changed to facilitate the passage of legislation through the house. He is very anxious to bring in his proposed legislation, and I personally would like to see the measure dealing with farm machinery.
The minister went on to say that his policies will vastly change the agricultural economy. I remember reading about the minister, at a meeting he had at Claresholm, Alberta, in the following day's Calgary Herald. I do not have the clipping here, but he said he had been farming for 15 or 18 years with a 1928 model tractor, and he felt this was good enough for all farmers, that farmers were being abused by the machinery salesmen, that they were over-buying machinery, and that the farm machinery agents were just taking advantage of them.
I just wonder what will be in this farm machinery legislation, coming from a minister who is supposed to have farmed 18 years with a 1928 model tractor and who said it was every bit as good as his neighbour's rubber tired tractor. I myself did quite a bit of farming with a 1928 tractor and with a team of horses, but when you compare the three modes there is no doubt that the rubber tired tractor is superior.

Supply-Agriculture
The minister also said at the Lethbridge meeting that as soon as the pension bill was passed through parliament his farm legislation would be presented. In a sense the pension bill has passed through parliament. It has been withdrawn and now we have a flag issue that also will eventually be withdrawn because Canada does not want two flags. It too will occupy the time of the house and keep this vastly important agricultural legislation from being proceeded with, and these smokescreens will continue until the minister makes up his mind as to what type of farm machinery bill he wants.
We have also noticed that the minister is greatly interested in improving his image. He has found out it is not too good across western Canada, particularly in Alberta. Therefore he has got a new assistant, a former member of the press gallery, who has written a letter, on the minister's stationery, to weekly newspapers in which, the assistant, Mr. Peacock, says:
He-
The minister
-is concerned that the people in your area have every chance to learn as authoritatively, objectively and comprehensively what their government is doing.
I am pleased to hear this because if it is going to be an authoritative weekly column this means the minister is going to spend more time in parliament, and if it is going to be objective and comprehensive, this means he is finally going to start comprehending his own department and parliament itself. In fact, I have a couple of copies of some news releases he has already issued, and it is interesting to note that in some respects he is bypassing one large branch in the Department of Agriculture, the information branch.
At what price are they being auctioned?
The minister is not as smart-I should not use that word-not as wise, or perhaps in such financial difficulty as the hon. member for Port Arthur, because he is giving these out to weekly papers free.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he realize this is not the information branch? It is the propaganda branch.

Well, if I were chairman I would rule that that was a statement I wholeheartedly agree with, rather than a question. But these releases are going to be interesting. I am told that some 20 weekly
(Mr. Horner (Acadia).]
newspapers already subscribe to the minister's weekly complimentary and authoritative report on parliament, and perhaps the Clerk of the House or someone else in this house could make a notation in each one of those weekly papers saying how often or how long the minister spent in parliament in order to grasp this information.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: The hon. member is notably away more than any other person.

Now we hear something from the authority on the rules over on that side of the house. There is no question but that I find myself extremely occupied and not in the house on occasions, but my voting record is there for everybody to see, and while I know it could be better I am still not ashamed of it.
The minister is trying to create an image. The other day he was still auctioning, but that was an auction engagement made some time ago. Recently, no one has made any comment on his auctioneering services. Oh, maybe I am a bit envious; maybe there is a bit of auctioneer in me, too. But I notice that on May 18 he auctioned a famous Holstein herd for an amount which totalled $323,000. I roughly figured out the commission on this at the rate of 15 per cent-I was told this by a contributor to one of the sales. It comes to $48,000, a nice day's work-
Hear, hear.

-and an honourable profession. But surely if the minister is going to report authoritatively and comprehensively on this parliament and the work of his department he should spend full time at it. There is a report with regard to his auctioneering services in the Western Producer of October 3, 1963. The Western Producer is, I may say, a well known rural farm paper. This is what the editorial had to say:
We can think of dozens of good reasons for Mr. Hays to be quite properly absent from the house, carrying out duties directly connected with his job as minister. Auctioning cattle isn't among them, no matter how good the cattle, nor if they are owned by senators and other prominent people. There are other auctioneers. The minister's first responsibility is to his job as minister.
That is why I began my remarks by pointing out that these estimates we are discussing today concern the largest single industry in Canada, the biggest employer in Canada and the life saver of 1963 with regard to Canada's financial situation. Yet the minister is more concerned with improving his own financial position than with looking after the biggest

single employer in Canada and the biggest single industry in Canada.
I think I should correct one or two of those statements.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the minister rising on a question of privilege?
Yes. I received nothing. There were 2,000 farmers there from 15 different countries. I was happy to be there and I discussed many problems with them. But I did not charge anything for my services.
What was your own farm income last year?

More than yours.
It is all very well for the minister to say he did not charge anything. How much did he receive, and how much will he be receiving?
On a question of privilege; I received nothing.

Only time will tell. How much is Romandale Farms obligated to the minister for selling those cattle? When is the next election coming, and how much will they contribute to his campaign fund or to the campaign fund of the Liberal party? Nobody in public life does $50,000 worth of business and says: "Don't pay me". They definitely feel obligated and will certainly make a contribution in respect of that obligation in the future. One may rest assured of that. This sale of Holsteins resulted in record prices. There is a full report of it here. To quote the minister's own words, only time will tell, and in this case only time will tell how much Romandale Farms are obligated.
The legislation which the minister hopes to put on the order paper has been advertised in many papers. One of the items deals with farm improvement loans. We had that on the order paper as far back as the spring of 1963 -it was intended to increase the amount which could be loaned under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Everyone knows we have been interested in the Farm Credit Corporation. We set it up, we got it working and we increased the grants from time to time. I am interested in this piece of legislation and in particular in what they intend to do with regard to interest rates in respect of it. Did they ever stop to think that it is fine and dandy to give a farmer $40,000 and charge him a huge rate of interest on that money while providing very little marketing information, very little marketing help to market his product in order to pay the debt? Forty
Supply-Agriculture
thousand dollars at 5 per cent interest-we can be certain they would not lend a farmer as much money as that without maintaining the present rate of interest; that comes to $2,000, no small sum.
I see in a newspaper clipping that the minister's farm machinery bill will be the saviour of the small farmer. He is making some small farmers big and maintaining others by giving them 1928 tractors, I would imagine. Forty thousand dollars at 6 per cent interest would come to nearly $2,400 a year in interest alone. Surely, the minister will give consideration to saving a farmer $400 a year in interest?
We have heard some talk about the length of time a farmer would have in which to repay his debt. Certainly, the period should be lengthened, but with the increasing length of time it becomes of the utmost importance that the interest rate should be maintained and should not be increased. Because of the time increase a farmer instead of paying back $40,000 will be paying back more like $80,000, if he takes the full time allotted to him under the proposal which the minister may or may not have in mind. Certainly he has suggested from time to time that the time should be increased along with the amount of the loan. Well, I am in full accord that the Farm Credit Corporation should be able to lend more money, but I would rather see many other changes in the legislation to allow the small farmer to get started, or add to the property he may now own. But, of course, we shall see the bill in due time and no doubt I shall have more to say when it is before us.
The recent image builder which the minister has in mind is that he plans to fly members of parliament to various farm regions. This is going to be an interesting junket. It should increase the tourist expenditure by Canadians in Canada. But what real purpose will be accomplished? Is the agriculture committee going to fly to New Brunswick, for example, and set up a day for a meeting, and will farmers be called in and be told: Here is the minister, here are the members; ask your questions and the minister will be glad to answer? Is this to be the purpose of the junket? Or are we to go around interviewing farmers throughout Canada and asking them what will help solve their problems? As a member of the committee I shall certainly be pleased to go along, but it will be a waste of the taxpayers' money because it is the minister who designates the legislation; it is the minister who puts it on the order

Supply-Agriculture
paper or does not put it on the order paper; it is the minister who brings in the useful legislation which will benefit various segments of the agricultural economy. If the minister wants to fly all around Canada, and he has done a considerable amount of it already, to bone up on the various farm problems, then I think that would be money well spent by the Canadian taxpayer. He might find some answers to a lot of the problems that have been troubling him and his government with regard to agriculture.
This was the party that was going to make decisions. Last fall the Minister of Agriculture told the farmers not to grow wheat: "We have enough of it." The Minister of Trade and Commerce told them not to grow any more wheat, that we were going to have enough of it. We were lucky to have this one big sale. The farmers have gone ahead and pretty well completed putting in one of the largest crops of wheat this country has ever seen. I think it will be in the neighbourhood of 30 million acres. Did they receive any advice from this government about markets, about whether or not it was wise to plant this wheat? At one time they were told by both ministers not to plant wheat. Then reports appeared in the newspapers that the Minister of Trade and Commerce said the outlook was good for wheat sales to Russia to continue; that Russia would continue to be a buyer of Canadian wheat. The Minister of Agriculture has backed away somewhat from his initial statement that farmers should go into other branches of agricultural production, such as beef cattle. The beef cattle industry does not look too good this spring, with a surplus in the United States, the country that sets our market price.
I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that this government, as it has done in connection with many pieces of legislation, has wobbled and waffled in giving advice to farmers with regard to markets for their products. Today we see the agriculture committe studying the tobacco industry. What is the purpose of that inquiry? It is to improve the image of the present government with the tobacco farmers in order to try to undo some of the harm the Minister of National Health and Welfare did from a political point of view. The government should be concerned about the tobacco industry. Many governments have been. The Ontario government just appointed a commission to study the industry. Why the concern all of a sudden about images? We have concern about the image of the party the

image of the Prime Minister, the image of the Department of Agriculture and the minister, as a prime concern of the government today. One would almost think they were preparing for an election.
Certainly the country does not want an election. I read in one of the newspapers today that the flag issue will bring about an election. This country has waited a number of years for a truly distinctive flag, if this is what people want to call this new version we are getting. Certainly we can wait another couple of years. The country does not want an election. Why be concerned about image building? Why has the Minister of Agriculture started issuing free press releases for the rural newspapers? Why do we have members of parliament flying all across Canada in this process of image building? There is no other reason than to make Harry, if I may use the term, look like one of the boys in relation to the agriculture committee and the members of this house. This is another effort at image building. Image building will not create the smokescreen that is desired by that party. As long as there is an opposition in this house, members will be able to clear away the smoke and see where the real action has been with regard to agriculture.

I shall not detain the committee long by the few remarks I have to make. It has been brought to my attention that a number of newspapers in my riding have received letters from Mr. Don Peacock, who I presume is an employee of the Department of Agriculture, which are characterized as reports from parliament hill. During the past six years that I have been a member of this house I have written articles on the debates which have occurred in parliament when, in my view, it was thought of public interest to do so. The custom has grown up for individual members to send reports from parliament hill to their own constituents. This practice has grown up over the years and is not something which I have popularized. I have simply taken it as a practice which has grown up. Certainly under no circumstances has it been the practice for a minister of the crown to try to improve his image by circulating, far and wide, the "Hays Report From Parliament Hill". This is plagiarism. If the minister had any thoughts of decency in relation to the private members of this house, he would reconsider his position in choosing a title which is reserved by custom and practice for hon. members.

If the minister wants to send the "Hays Report From Parliament Hill" to the constituents of Calgary South, no one could find fault. However, if he wants to employ somebody on his staff, who is receiving $12,000 a year, to make up a report to send far and wide as the "Hays Report From Parliament Hill", while he is out conducting auction sales and has not heard what has taken place on parliament hill surely his constituents will not think well of that. What are the people of the country going to think? I would suggest, for his own self-respect, that the hon. member from Calgary South reconsider his position. If he does not, then I am certain the criticism he is going to receive will more than balance the benefits which he might think he is going to receive by way of improving his image as Minister of Agriculture. The minister's popularity is at a very low ebb, make no mistake about that.
I understand the minister has a ranch in my riding of Macleod. I have heard it said that in the next election he intends to run in the Macleod riding. I shall be delighted to have him as an opponent. If he does, I might say that he had better lengthen his legs if he is going to run against me. It will probably fall on the shoulders of this Conservative party to clean up this whole mess in agriculture which he has created. We shall be able to do it. Let me say that every Liberal who has run in the Macleod riding in the past three elections has lost his deposit, so he is welcome to be in the same category.
I should like to say that there are many things about the minister's department which should be mentioned, but I do not wish to repeat the things to which other members have referred.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask about the Chain lakes project out of Claresholm. We have been working on that project for some five years. There was some question whether this project should be at Chain lakes or at the Flying E, and after P.F.R.A. had made their surveys of Chain lakes it was decided to wait until the department had examined other sites. Now at last the local people have agreed to go ahead at Chain lakes. The engineering studies have been completed and the minister has said yes, we will go ahead at the Chain lakes site.
However, in this year's estimates I understand from checking with the department officials that all that is being done this year is to carry out certain studies. There will be
Supply-Agriculture
no bulldozers getting to work, there will be no construction work; only a small token amount of the estimates before us are devoted to this purpose, just enough to make surveys. In other words, the department does not intend to do anything this year at Chain lakes; and if that is the case the minister should tell the people at Claresholm and at Granum, who are depending on the Minister of Agriculture to get busy, how much of this project is to be completed this year. The minister has said that this project is going to be completed in 1965, which is more than a year away. In other words, he is going to do nothing this year. He is going to wait and see whether or not it rains. That is the situation; and make no mistake, Mr. Minister of Agriculture, the people of Claresholm and the people of Granum who depend on the storage of water in Willow Creek are expecting something more important and more definite than this.
Whom were they depending on two years ago?

They were depending on the government in power at that time, which initiated the study by P.F.R.A. which brought in a report on the Chain lakes project. It was also recommended by the council of Willow Creek municipality that the Flying E site be re-examined, and at the suggestion of Willow Creek municipality the government postponed any construction at Chain lakes until the alternative site at the Flying E was properly examined.
These are the facts, Mr. Chairman. The minister can smile, look fat and prosperous and everything else-

speechtext: The pot is calling the kettle black.

-but these are the facts, and the people out there, do not forget, are watching what the Minister of Agriculture is trying to do. But they are having a hard time trying to see anything at all that he is doing. I shall be out at the Cartwright ranch on Sunday at a big old timers picnic. I shall be out near the minister's ranch, and since I am a lifetime member of the old timers association in that area I would extend an invitation to him to be my guest. I should be glad to pick him up and bring him over to the Cartwright ranch if he is in that part of the area. We might be good friends as individuals outside the House of Commons, but I want to tell him this, that the policies of this government will certainly not

Supply-Agriculture be tolerated or accepted by the people in my riding, or for that matter any of the people in the other agricultural ridings of this country. Regardless of what the minister may do by way of writing articles to improve his image, he is going to find difficulty in correcting the image of this government and the record of the present Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I have been sitting here this afternoon hoping really that item 1 would be passed and that we could get on with the details of the estimates. Seeing that that is not likely I want to make a few kindly observations. I have read the minister's speech in opening his estimates and I have read his speech on the occasion of the amendment on going into supply last Monday, but I must say I fail to see in either of those speeches the sort of reply I should like to the requests of farm organizations in many respects.
We note that there is going to be an amendment to the Farm Credit Act, which we are pleased about. We also note that there is going to be an amendment to the Bankruptcy Act, which the farmers will be very interested in, because they have suffered losses. We also note that more active consideration is being given to the ARDA program than has been the case for some time. However, I wish the minister would give the committee his reaction, before these estimates are concluded, to the representations of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture with regard to the world food program and with respect to taxation policy. We should like to know what he is doing within the cabinet in this regard.
The federation presented to the Minister of Finance immediately following its annual meeting a submission containing recommendations on excise and sales tax and customs tariffs on goods which enter into the farmers' cost of production. We should like to know the reaction of the minister to these recommendations. Page 9 of the brief presented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the Prime Minister of Canada and the members of the cabinet on February 26, 1964, reads, in part, as follows:
In a somewhat different field, we would like to draw your attention to the resolution in appendix K in which we ask both provincial and federal governments to work out means of ending the use of property taxes for financing local education costs, and instead find means of ensuring that federal funds are made available for education in amounts which will ensure that financing needs for education in Canada are adequately and equitably met.


We should like to know the reaction of the minister to this representation in connection with property taxes. I think this is a nationwide request on the part of the farmers of Canada. I know it is a matter which is brought up at every provincial convention of agricultural organizations and it has been the subject of discussion throughout the years.
We should also like to hear the minister's attitude toward this particular problem, because the burden is increasing every year, owing to the increasing cost of taxation, the need for new and better schools, more teachers, and so on, all of which we support.
Then we should like to know the minister's views with respect to the representations concerning pension plans. Paragraph 25 of the brief states:
We would hope to be submitting to you more detailed views and recommendations on this subject of pension plans. At this time there is one central point of policy on which we would like to be very emphatic. We think it is essential that, from the first, participation in the plan should be mandatory not only for employees, but also for self-employed persons.
I mention that because I have had some correspondence from the farmers in my own constituency who are concerned with this aspect of the Canada pension plan. We should like to know whether the minister supports the proposals of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and other farm organizations in this respect.
Then we should like to know the minister's attitude toward the federation's proposal with respect to the St. Lawrence seaway. In paragraph 29 of their brief the federation submits that:
Our federation opposes any increase in St. Lawrence seaway tolls, or any Welland canal tolls whatever.
Then we should like to know the minister's reply to the question of unemployment insurance for farm labour. This matter has been brought up as a private measure by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale. We all give him full credit for it. He is a good representative. He knows how to represent farmers. He has his feet on the ground instead of his head in the air. Paragraph 44 is headed "Unemployment Insurance for Farm Labour" and reads as follows:
We appreciate that the government must now be very intensively examining the findings of the royal commission on unemployment insurance, and planning new legislation. What we wish to emphasize is that there are many farmer employers who are at a distinct disadvantage in the labour market created by the lack of coverage for farm workers. This is a very serious matter for many farmers and

very unsatisfactory also for the man who would otherwise like to enter farm work. Our request is that, without delay, insurance be extended on a compulsory basis to farm employees in particular, defined geographical areas or industry groupings. This we believe should be done when requested by groups of farmers in a particular area or producing a particular commodity.
We wholeheartedly support that request. I know a number of farmers in my constituency who have been unable to obtain good employees who would have liked to work for them and who would have preferred to do farm work, but because of the lack of unemployment insurance in this field these workers have had to go into occupations where they could get their insurance stamps and their benefits later on, if necessary.
We would like to know what the minister thinks. We think that the Minister of Agriculture should rise in this house as the representative of the farmers of this country and say that he believes in this idea, and then behind the scenes in the cabinet he should be doing his best to get the Minister of Labour to see eye to eye with the farmers of Canada.
I have one other question to raise which is of interest to the fruit growing industry of British Columbia. It has to do with certain resolutions passed at the 75th annual convention of the British Columbia fruit growers association which was held at Kelowna on January 21, 22 and 23, 1964. There are a number of resolutions of interest here but I want to draw two particularly to the minister's attention. I have had some personal knowledge of fruit growing over a period of 50 years, but have had to go out of it in recent years. One reason for having to do so is the fact that men employed in this work are not covered by unemployment insurance. I wish to refer to resolution No. 39, diseases and insects of pome fruits, which was introduced by the Keremeos local of our organization. It reads as follows:
Whereas pest and disease control on apples and pears is a major problem throughout the industry, and
Whereas costs of spray materials are steadily rising with tolerances of spray residue being ever more rigorously controlled, and
Whereas there is an excellent publication by the Canadian Department of Agriculture, "No. 915, Diseases, Insects and Mites of Stone Fruits", available to growers, and
Whereas there is at present no publication available on diseases, insects and mites on apples and pears,
Therefore be it resolved by this 1964 B.C.F.G.A. convention that the B.C.F.G.A. apply for such a publication, namely, "Diseases and Insects and Mites on Apples and Pears and Their Control".

The next resolution, No. 40, is related to that resolution. It has to do with non-chemical insect control and reads as follows:
Whereas we appreciate the work already being done on the control of insect pests by non-chemical means, and inasmuch as the need for such control increases as insects rapidly develop resistance to chemical sprays, so that new and costly materials are continually required to replace materials which have become ineffective,
Therefore be it resolved by this 1964 B.C.F.G.A. convention that the federal Department of Agriculture be requested to accelerate research into non-chemical insect control increasing appropriations for this work if necessary.
I do not want to delay the passage of item 1 but I do ask the minister to give consideration to the representations of the farm organizations including the last two resolutions I have read.
I will be very pleased to do that.

Before item 1 goes through I should like the minister to agree that I may discuss crop insurance under the P.F.A.A. heading. As the minister knows, there is no item in the estimates for crop insurance because it comes under supplementaries. I trust it will be all right with the minister if I raise the question of crop insurance under the P.F.A.A. heading, vote 15.
Yes.

Second, I would ask the minister to facilitate the work of the opposition and save our having to ask questions by requesting the department to take each of the votes and give us a list of the major increases and the major decreases, not the small ones but the ones that are sizeable, so that we may have a more complete breakdown than appears in the estimates. If that can be given to us before we next study these estimates I think it will facilitate their passage.
The hon. member wants the increase or decrease in each vote?
Just the major increases and decreases. If there is an increase of over 10 per cent in an item let us have the increase and what caused it and the same thing for the decreases.
We will be glad to do that.

Mr. Chairman, I believe that farming falls in a very special category in Canada. In fact, it is the most important profession in Canada, and I think it would be worth while to consider it for a few moments and fully analyse the problems facing farmers, in view of the economic stagnation existing in the country.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the house for its kindness and I will do my best to be brief.
For the past few days, that is the period just referred to by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), the various problems facing our farmers have been under consideration.
In my opinion, farmers know quite well how to solve their production problems. Indeed, they are assisted in that by their professional associations, organizations and unions which have at their disposal the necessary means to look into these problems.
But another problem which must be urgently settled has to do with the sale of the production. Farmers must not only produce, but they also have to dispose of their production at a reasonable price which will enable them to meet their other obligations.
In the past, people were inclined to think that anyone could be a farmer; this opinion

is still current in some circles. I do not agree with that. Today, farming methods are changing more and more, and a farmer must necessarily be conversant with agriculture and moveover be a businessman. In fact, he has to make purchases and if he is not well up in business, he is liable to be cheated sometimes.
In addition, he must have salesmanship; he must know the tricks of the trade in order to make profits. He must also have some knowledge of mechanics, welding and a whole lot of trades; otherwise, he has to make expenditures which are hard on his budget.
In my opinion, contrary to members of all but a few other professions, a true farmer has a variety of skills and that is why he deserves more consideration from the people of Canada. He should be shown greater respect and his income should enable him to enjoy a standard of living comparable to that of any other class of citizens.
There is another point which is of special interest to my riding, that of Chapleau, and that is the situation of farmers under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I would like for a moment to draw the attention of the minister on this matter. I know it will also interest the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), but as we are considering the agriculture estimates, I hope the Minister of Agriculture will take due note of it.
In my constituency, farming is far from being a thriving business and, often, the owner of a farm or a plot of land has to find outside work for several months each year. During the period where our farmers work mainly as lumbermen, they have to contribute to the unemployment insurance fund. They often work five, six and even seven months a year away from the farm, but when work in the forest ends, some time in the spring, they are perhaps out of work for a few weeks before farm operations begin. Then, our farmers have to face many difficulties when they wish to draw unemployment benefits. I think it would be advisable to consider the situation more carefully and give the farmer who has a low income the privileges granted other classes of society.
I will not deal further with this matter this evening, in order to allow this first item to be passed. I will make other remarks as the various items are submitted to us.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESTRAINT OF USE
PROVISION FOR RESTRAINT OF USE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-32, to restrain the use of tobacco.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the aim of this bill is to safeguard the public against misleading claims by manufacturers and distributors of tobacco products. The bill and the proposition contained therein is in line with similar legislation being advanced at this time in the United States by the federal trade commission. Part I of the bill sets forth that it is a finable offence to sell or furnish tobacco products to children under 16 years of age. However, that part of the bill is presently an act and was enacted as early as 1908. The only reason it is in the bill I am putting forward is to avoid having two acts on the same general subject. Part II of the bill, which is the new part, would empower the government to control, in the cause of public health, the labelling, exposing, advertising or promoting of tobacco products, much as we now control the same activities in regard to food and drug standards through the food and drug legislation.
Hon. members are, I am sure, well aware of the steps which have been taken in recent years by many other governments in this phase of public health protection. Such countries as Great Britain, France, the Scandinavian countries, the Soviet union and Italy have taken some action to curb the toll of cigarette disease. In connection with this, Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) for her action and the leadership she has given, she being the first minister in the federal field in Canada to encourage study and action toward curbing abuses connected with the excessive consumption of cigarettes. As we know, she called a national conference last year at which were represented, I think, all the provincial health departments in Canada, the tobacco industry and other organizations which are concerned with the toll taken by cigarettes.
Restraint of Use of Tobacco
In passing I would like to say that our provincial government in British Columbia, with which I certainly differ in many other respects, is nevertheless to be commended for having pioneered political action in this field. The minister of health of British Columbia, Hon. Eric Martin, as much as three years ago took an active part in getting provincial action to establish, first of all, funds for educational efforts directed to our younger people to acquaint them with the various tolls taken by excessive smoking of cigarettes. As a matter of fact this next week will mark the fourth annual non-smoking day in British Columbia, which is sponsored by the provincial government of that province.
I am sure hon. members will be aware of the pressing nature of the findings of such organizations as the Royal College of Physicians in Great Britain, the American cancer society, the Canadian Medical Association and several other organizations of that type in regard to exposing the dangers connected with the excessive use of tobacco products. The most recent expose has been by the United States medical authority, with which we are all familiar.
On this point, and in passing, I would like to call to the attention of hon. members that the only interest these impartial medical authorities have in bringing forward the reports they have brought forward, exposing the dangers of excessive cigarette consumption, is that of public health. They have nothing else to sell. They are not concerned with producing tobacco, advertising it, selling it or displaying it. They are only concerned with helping to maintain and improve the standards of public health. They are impartial in that respect.
Mr. Speaker, there have been many activities under way in the last year or two in line with this general program of combating disease from tobacco products, and I have a quotation or two which I would like to make from a pamphlet which is being circulated just now in Washington state by an organization called the "Governor's Conference on Smoking and Youth." There is to be a meeting next week at Seattle, Washington, a conference on smoking and youth, to be attended by 20 health and youth groups concerned in protecting young people from death and disease from the excessive use of tobacco, particularly cigarettes. I quote from the pamphlet as follows:
If one adds all of the deaths from auto accidents in the U.S.A., about 40,000 in 1963, all of the deaths from suicide, about 20,000, all of the deaths
