In speaking to this Bill No. C-32, an act to restrain the use of tobacco, may I say at once that I am entirely in accord with part I-the present act to restrain the use of tobacco by young persons. I should like to say, further, that the tobacco industry also believes that this
Restraint of Use of Tobacco part of the bill is a good one, and has for years believed it to be so. Records show that the tobacco industry is in full support of its intent and purposes and has always done its best to co-operate in any activity designed to promote its observance.
Part II of the bill is another matter. In plain words it will be applied to restrain the use of tobacco in Canada. Clause 13 in particular gives to the governor in council a terrific power-the power to make regulations respecting the labelling, the packaging, the selling, the distributing, the offering, the exposing-whatever that may mean; I do not know-the importing, the testing and the analysis of tobacco in addition to what other regulations may be considered fitting-if there are any other matters left to regulate. Certainly, the adoption of this bill would constitute an entirely unwarranted interference by the government in the affairs of an industry which has always been law abiding and, as I have stated on previous occasions, an industry to which the government owes much from the point of view of revenue and employment. Actually, many of the items which this bill seeks to regulate are already covered by laws having to do with customs and excise, and the regulations made thereunder.
Concerning advertising, section 306 of the Criminal Code already exists to deal with false, deceptive and misleading advertising. This does not relate to tobacco only; it covers all products. In the circumstances it would seem that additional and special regulations to govern tobacco advertising specifically would be discriminatory and inequitable. I should like at this time to correct a wrong impression which people have towards advertising relating to cigarettes or the promotion of cigarette sales. There are four companies manufacturing cigarettes in Canada and these four companies spend approximately between $15 million and $18 million annually on promoting and advertising. The first impression from these figures is to think they represent a tremendous amount of money and that the tobacco companies are really "going to town". However, cigarette advertising amounts, in fact, to less than 3 per cent of total sales value as compared with 9 per cent in the case of proprietary drugs, 8 per cent for soaps-the good old soap opera, and Dr. Kildare-and 7 per cent with regard to alcoholic beverages, the latter figure being about 2J times the amount spent on cigarette advertising. That is our dear old friend John Barleycorn. I am sure members

Restraint of Use of Tobacco will agree that these figures show that cigarette advertising volume is consistent with the competitive situation and is not disproportionate or overdone, as many have been led to believe.	.	.
To turn, now, to one of the points raised by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather), perhaps I could quote what was said by Mr. Keith, president of the Imperial Tobacco Company of Canada with respect to the voluntary self-regulating code recently announced by the cigarette manufacturers in the United States. He stated that the code appears to be a realistic move in terms of the situation in that country and is evidence of the desire of the industry to co-operate with the appropriate authorities. I should like to go into a little more detail and quote one or two excerpts from this code, because I have an idea which I wish to develop. They are as follows:
1.	Cigarette advertising shall not appear on T.V. and radio programs or in publications directed primarily to persons under 21 years of age;
2.	Cigarette advertising shall not represent that cigarette smoking is essential to social prominence, distinction, success or sexual attraction.
Incidentally, all models used must be over 25 years of age and this practice has been followed in Canada for some time.
3.	Cigarette advertising shall not depict as a smoker any person well known as being or having been an athlete.
I wonder if as much can be said with regard to the advertising of other products. The other night I watched a television show sponsored by a certain product that is doing more damage to the people of this country than the cigarette or smoking industry. This position regarding the prowess of athletes and problems of social distinction was taken in connection with this problem. I am not going to mention any names, but you can judge for yourselves. In Canada, we have already moved our television program to 9 p.m.
I should like to deal with labelling. The suggested labelling proposals in this bill appear to be based on the assumption that the hypotheses linking smoking and various human diseases have been proven. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather) has already stated that it has not yet been proven. He has given certain illustrations that he feels are O.K. However, I want to say that the ingredient or ingredients in tobacco or tobacco smoke said to be causing cancer have not yet been isolated or proven to be the cause. The labelling of tobacco products as indicated in the bill would not only be illogical but also very unrealistic,


unscientific and therefore misleading. The mere listing of the constituents of tobacco smoke would have no meaning to the consumer or purchaser of tobacco products. If they are not producing the cancer, why should they be put on the label? At the same time such labelling, meaningless as it may be, would unjustly be placing a sort of stigma on the tobacco products themselves.
We have read about the report of the advisory committee to the surgeon general of the public health service of the United States. Like my hon. friend, I can quote reams and reams of statistics. However, the attitude toward cigarette smoking has undergone a big change since this report first came out. I should like to say that we are now reading such headlines as "Cigarettes are safer now, say cancer scientists". Dr. Ernest L. Wynder and Dr. Dietrich Hoffman, of the Sloan Kettering Institute, New York city, say that the majority of filter tip cigarettes now contain less cancer inducing properties than cigarettes formerly did. Dr. Wynder was one of the members of the first research group to point to an association between cigarette smoking and lung cancer. Now, he has made the statement to which I have just referred.
It was pointed out also that different types of tobacco used in cigarettes have made a difference. This brings to the fore again the fact that more money and time should be devoted to research, as I mentioned in my motion two weeks ago.
Many statements that have been made, and are still being made, in this anti-cigarette smoking campaign have been proven to be erroneous. It seems too bad that a number of these statements have been made by men of good repute who are dealing with something outside their field of endeavour. When a person deals with something outside his own field of endeavour, he is generally running into trouble. For example, Dr. R. G. Williams is reported by the Calgary Herald as having stated:
The percentage of arsenic, a cancer causing agent, has been increasing year by year in tobacco as a result of insect spraying.
I am going to say that nothing could be further from the truth, and I will tell you why. This is something about which I happen to know a little bit. In Canada, little or no arsenic has been used as a spray or otherwise in the tobacco fields for the past 10 to 15 years. Proof of this is the fact that in Canadian cigarettes the arsenic level in tobacco smoke is one part per million, well below

the five parts per million allowed by the Canada Food and Drugs Act. I am not saying that such statements are made by one side only. Possibly they are made by both sides. However, when they are made by men with an M.D. after their names, the average person takes that statement as definite proof.
It may be all right for the federal authorities to sponsor a report on smoking, but it is quite another matter for them to try to control the habit. If they are sincere in trying to protect the people against themselves, then let us not forget that we are trying to protect people against themselves. They decide they want to smoke. They decide they want to take a drink. They decide they want to have ten cups of coffee per day. They decide they want to eat certain things, and this is their business. This is not the government's business. The government can advise them not to do it, but the government cannot force them to stop it.
Let us remember that most experts concede that urban air pollution, which is carbon monoxide, probably possesses much the same peril, and efforts to control it have not been noticeably successful. Because of this peril, are we going to say that the government should dismantle those industries which contribute to air pollution?
Then, there is that good old friend of ours that I should like to mention once more, old John Barleycorn. I have not anything against John-I mean John Barleycorn. However, it is estimated that there are some 250,000 alcoholics in Canada. If one includes their families, this means that there are perhaps a million persons affected by alcoholism. Then, there is cirrhosis of the liver, and other diseases that are brought on by alcoholism. If everybody is sincere in protecting people against themselves, why do they select one product in connection with which to take action? Most hon. members may have heard of North Carolina's most illustrious son, the late Joseph Daniels, who was a real fighter against alcohol and a real fighter against smoking. At one time he said that he never knew a man to beat his wife because he smoked.
There still remains that controversial subject of cholesterol. Are we going to put in legislation to stop people from eating butter, eggs or putting cream in their coffee? Every one of these products contribute to cholesterol. Here is something that is very interesting, and I know hon. members will be interested in it. Not only is the brain rich in cholesterol but cholesterol contains the same nucleus as sex hormones and, therefore,

Restraint of Use of Tobacco is not to be deprecated. My gosh, perish the thought. I can see an unproductive generation in the future if you give the government too much power.
Finally I want to ask hon. members, including the hon. member for New Westminster, if they realize what it will mean if this bill is passed? It will give the governor in council complete power and control over every individual connected directly or indirectly with the tobacco business. If you look at it closely, you will realize it is just about as bad as, if not worse than the recent police bill introduced by Hon. Frederick Cass in the Ontario legislature. If this bill is passed it will be the first step toward doing away with everything for which democracy stands, from freedom of speech to the freedom of free enterprise, with free enterprise competing as it should under laws that are equal for all. I feel sure that the governor in council would hate like the very old dickens to try to implement this bill.
In conclusion, I just want to say that this type of bill gives far too much power and control to the governor in council.

I did not say anything about the doctors. I said that a doctor made a statement in a field he knew nothing about. I do not want to take away anything from the doctors, because I have the highest respect for the medical association. subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESTRAINT OF USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-32, if passed, would endeavour to restrain the use of tobacco by young persons under the age of 16 years. It also provides certain penalties for offences under the act committed by those persons who sell or furnish cigarettes, cigarette papers, or tobacco in other forms. The penalty applies to those

Restraint of Use of Tobacco under 16 who may be found smoking or chewing tobacco in streets or public places.
The hon. member has long been interested in endeavouring to restrain the smoking of tobacco by juveniles and those not so juvenile, and this part of the bill I commend. I think we are all quite concerned at the use of tobacco among our young people, those between 12 and 17 years of age. I also think we are quite concerned why these young people are forming these smoking habits in their early teens.
I was interested in a clipping I picked up headed "Survey finds smoking habit increasing among teenagers". The article is written by a Mr. Jack Hutton and says in part:
The number of Canadian teenagers hooked for life on smoking is increasing every day, according to a survey by this column.
This phenomenon is happening every day in every city, town or village in Canada-despite the strongest warning campaign we've ever known.
A Vancouver 14-year-old girl summed it up. "If you don't accept a cigarette, you aren't counted as one of the group. And who wants to be out?"
Very few teenagers have what it takes to "be out", according to our correspondents. The same pattern showed up all across the country: Teenagers aren't listening to warnings about the dangers of smoking.
The question came up several months ago when I mentioned the fact that the Canadian cancer society and several other groups are worried that smoking seems to be a status symbol for teenagers.
A small pin for those who decided to bypass smoking was produced several months ago. But I personally have never noticed one on anyone. What happened to the pins I don't know.
I think the hon. member who introduced this bill this afternoon was one of those who was endeavouring to provide pins for non-smokers. The article continues:
The first letters answering the column were all from readers who scoffed at warnings about smoking. This didn't bother me-at first. What did alarm me was that no one spoke up for the other side.	.
Therefore, several friends have conducted private surveys during the last three months. Each kept a small notebook handy during August, September and October, quietly jotting down opinions of their friends.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these are some of the opinions:
What emerged were capsule comments from almost 500 teenagers, ranging in age from 13 to 19. Many said they were already smoking "a pack a day" by the age of 15. Some had developed the habit by 13.
Here's what a Winnipeg 16-year-old boy had to say. "The warnings we hear would be a lot more impressive if we didn't see adults disregarding their own advice every minute of the day."
"The Canadian Medical Association frowns on smoking but the heaviest smoker I know is a doctor who lives close to us. And I could never

place much stock in what my folks said because they'd die without a morning cigarette."
A Halifax 17-year-old girl was one person who didn't smoke. But she added: "I was in a restaurant the other day sitting next to a booth where a girl was taking a merciless kidding from friends because she didn't smoke.
"Every time they lit up a cigarette, someone would offer her one and act surprised when she refused. They were calling her 'Mama's girl,' and I even think her boy friend was embarrassed.
"Finally, just before I left, the poor girl took a cigarette. They all broke out in cheers and her date beamed from ear to ear. What a sad thing to see."
I asked my correspondents to ask whether advertising was the main factor in influencing their friends. Very few said that it was. The gang was a far more important factor in almost every case.
From that article it seems that the people to educate are the parents of young children. With both mother and father in many cases working today, it seems to me that there is very little surveillance given the children in the teenage class. They are left pretty well to roam as they please and they naturally fall under the influence of older persons and especially of cigarette smokers.
If this bill were passed, applying these penalties, especially to those under 16 smoking in the street or a public place, does not seem to me to be the answer. You will drive them underground. If these penalties are enforced these people will go into a secluded place, a cellar or backyard to carry on their smoking habits. That is not what we wish to accomplish. I was interested in a news report this morning to the effect that one of our prominent tobacco companies hoped that within an 18-month period they would be able to produce a cigarette on the market with all possible causes of lung cancer removed from it. I hope this can be accomplished within a lesser period of time than that. I know that all our tobacco companies are doing research work in an attempt to find what are the main possible causes of lung cancer in so far as cigarettes are concerned, and they have spent thousands and thousands of dollars in research programs of their own.
At the present time our agriculture committee is studying the production of tobacco, and I hope that when their report is brought in it will recommend that sufficient money be set aside to enable research to be carried out by the Department of Agriculture into possible causes of lung cancer. The tobacco growers will also welcome that research. The tobacco companies would wish to co-operate 100 per cent in that type of work, and I am sure that everyone across the country would appreciate such studies.

I was also interested in another article by a prominent writer, a person by the name of Scott Young of the Globe and Mail. Scott Young apparently has a couple of teenage boys and he has used various methods in an attempt to stop them smoking. I think hon. members might be interested in a few extracts from this article.
Mr. Young says:
I can't think of a better way to bring on an acute case of restiveness among taxpayers than Wednesday's report that we are going to spend $600,000 of public money to discourage cigarette smoking.
Incidentally, this article appeared in the Globe and Mail of November 29, 1963. He goes on to say:
This is going to be divided as follows: $400,000 to tell youngsters that smoking is bad for them and $200,000 for research into why people start smoking and don't stop.
Couldn't we possibly find some way to tell youngsters, equally uselessly, that smoking is bad for them without it costing $400,000? I have an impulse to suggest that this anti-cigarette message be worked into beer commercials, but I guess I'd better not.
Miss Judy LaMarsh, Minister of National Health and Welfare (or, on alternate days, of national health and hellfire) announced this effective new method of throwing money down the drain after the closing session of the Canadian conference on smoking and health.
She said the educational program would not try to scare the children. This seems reasonable. You tell them that if they don't give up the weed they'll be dead at 40. They look around at the world of atomic weapons, death rates on highways, and all the other ways they might wind up dead by 40 anyway and they say, "So what else is new?"
They don't pay any more attention to the lung cancer threat than boys and girls of my generation did to being told that cigarettes would stunt their growth.
Miss LaMarsh has suggested that one method of persuasion might be an advertising campaign in which noted athletes and other celebrities tell why they don't smoke. This would not be worth the powder to blow it up. The same advertising agencies who picked up the loose change on the anticigarette campaign would be busy in another part of the office churning out ads in which athletes and other celebrities endorsed certain brands of cigarettes. This they'll do just as rapidly as they'll endorse a breakfast food, if the price is right.
If it has any pertinence here, I smoke, but not cigarettes. My two sons do. I tried every parental gambit to discourage them. With one, at the age of 14 or 15, every time I saw him smoking I had him write out a $2 cheque and forward it to the society for retarded children, and made sure that the subtlety was not lost on him. He kept on smoking.
The fact is that children have been fed antismoking propaganda ever since cigarettes were invented. It has had no effect at all. Their heroes smoke. Their heroines smoke. Even their parents, who fall into neither category but have a certain influence in some households, usually smoke. So some young people of considerable common sense
Restraint of Use of Tobacco smoke, and so do some stupid ones. It's a habit they acquire from adults-
One encouraging piece of information indicating that maybe tobacco can be put to a better use than smoking is an article headed, "Don't Tell Judy, But Pigs Thrive on Nip of Nicotine". Possibly we have at. last found an agricultural use for tobacco in. providing nicotine in pig feed. The article reads as follows:
It makes them attractively leaner and saves on food, say the results of tests conducted at the Nappan, N.S., research station of the federal agriculture department. Net profit was $1.30 to $1.70 higher for each animal taking nicotine than for porkers who didn't.
Dr. Hugh M. Cunningham of the Nappan station began seven years ago to try and produce a leaner pig. Now, says a department report, he has found that nicotine stimulates the release of a hormone from the adrenal glands which trims fat and increases the growth of the lean tissue much desired for bacons and hams. Thus, simply by adding five parts per one million of nicotine sulfate, the test pigs showed these desirable changes.
In closing I wish to commend the hon. member for introducing the bill. As I said at the beginning, if the bill were passed it would not have the desired effects but would create the possibility of more than ever driving our young people underground to carry on their smoking habits.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the three or four minutes left to me I want to say that as far as the first part of the bill is concerned there is apparently unanimous agreement throughout the house that this is a good piece of legislation. If they do not agree with what is written in the legislation, at least all of those who have taken part in this debate agree that it is desirable to discourage our young people from starting to smoke and acquiring a habit that they cannot leave. The motive behind this part of the bill, of course, is to discourage young people from smoking when they are young so that they will not be habitual smokers when they grow up.
There are some contradictions in the actions that have been taken by the present and former federal governments with respect to tobacco. I think it is fair to say that all members of the house-I know the members of our party would-would unanimously support the providing of additional funds for research to find a way of producing what might be called safe cigarettes, if such a thing can be found. I am not suggesting that any good purpose is served so far as the human body is concerned in people smoking, but I think we must face up to the fact that people do

Business of the House
smoke and probably will continue to do so. Therefore, for the good of the nation additional funds should be provided for research along this line.
1 know that we have authorized something like $600,000 for the purpose of educating our young people to refrain from taking up the habit in the first instance, while on the other hand we are spending funds through the agricultural stabilization board for the production of tobacco and also on research to enhance the production of tobacco. This may seem inconsistent, but it is not if we consider other products. There are other products with regard to which we pay money out of the federal treasury in the form of subsidies to assist production and at the same time we also make payments out of the federal treasury to get rid of the surpluses that are produced.
I see it is very close to six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I simply want to say that we are in favour of the first part of the bill, but so far as the second part is concerned I would say that while it may seem desirable, I think that from a practical point of view we would be far better to spend our money in trying to find some way that tobacco can be used safely, if such a way exists.
